en.title: Banks and how money is created
objectives: Read a simple bank balance sheet
Explain how bank lending creates deposits
Describe what limits money creation and why bank runs happen

learn.body: A bank takes deposits, makes loans and runs the payment system. It earns the gap between what it charges borrowers and pays depositors. Because only a small share of depositors withdraw on any day, a bank can lend most of the money it holds while keeping some in reserve.

A bank's assets are what it owns or is owed: loans, government securities, reserves at the central bank and cash. Its liabilities are what it owes: mainly customers' deposits and borrowing. The difference is equity, the owners' capital, which absorbs losses if loans go bad.

When a bank makes a loan, it credits the borrower's account with a new deposit. No one else's deposit falls. This is how most money in a modern economy is created. When loans are repaid, that money disappears. So the amount of money depends heavily on how much banks lend.

Banks keep reserves at the central bank to settle payments with each other. Many central banks set a minimum, the statutory reserve ratio. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka's ratio has been 2% of deposits since 2020. The textbook money multiplier links reserves to deposits, but in practice lending is limited more by demand, profitability, capital and regulation.

Narrow money (M1) is cash plus current account deposits. Broad money adds savings and fixed deposits: Sri Lanka publishes M2 and M2b. Watching the growth of broad money and private credit helps central banks judge whether demand is too strong or too weak.

Banks must hold capital, their own funds, as a share of their risk-weighted assets under rules based on the Basel framework. More capital means a bank can absorb losses without failing. Regulators also set liquidity rules so that banks can meet withdrawals.

If depositors fear a bank will fail, they may all try to withdraw at once. Even a healthy bank cannot repay everyone instantly, because its money is lent out. Deposit insurance, central bank lending in a crisis and strong supervision reduce the risk of runs. Silicon Valley Bank in the US collapsed in 2023 after a fast, online run.

en.title: Inflation and price indices
objectives: Calculate inflation from a price index, year on year and month on month
Explain basket weights and why food matters so much in South Asia
Identify who gains and who loses from inflation

learn.body: Inflation is the rate at which the general price level rises. It is usually measured as the change in a consumer price index over twelve months. Some prices always rise and others fall; inflation is about the average.

A consumer price index tracks the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services. Weights come from household spending surveys. Sri Lanka's CCPI and NCPI currently use 2021 as their base year, with weights from household surveys. Food has a much larger weight in poorer countries than in rich ones, so food prices drive inflation more.

learn.h: Year on year and month on month
learn.body: Year-on-year inflation compares this month with the same month last year; it is the headline figure. Month-on-month changes show recent momentum but are noisy and seasonal. A large month-on-month jump can keep year-on-year inflation high for a full year, until it drops out of the comparison.

Headline inflation covers the whole basket. Core inflation removes volatile items such as fresh food, energy and administered prices, to show the underlying trend. Central banks look at core to judge whether price pressure is spreading through the economy.

Prices rise when demand grows faster than the economy can produce (demand-pull), when costs such as fuel, wages or imports rise (cost-push), or when money supply grows much faster than output. Expectations matter too: if workers and firms expect high inflation, they raise wages and prices in advance.

Unexpected inflation hurts savers, people on fixed incomes and pensioners, and helps borrowers with fixed-rate debt, because debts shrink in real terms. It also redistributes from people who cannot raise their prices or wages to those who can. Poor households, who spend most on food, usually suffer most.

Falling prices can sound good, but persistent deflation makes debts heavier in real terms and can lead people to delay spending. Japan struggled with very low inflation and deflation for two decades. Most central banks therefore aim for low positive inflation, around 2% in rich countries and somewhat higher in many emerging economies.

en.title: What central banks do: CBSL, RBI, Fed
objectives: Compare the mandates of the CBSL, the RBI and the US Federal Reserve
Explain the main tools of monetary policy
Explain why central bank independence and communication matter

learn.body: A central bank issues currency, sets monetary policy, supervises banks, runs or oversees the payment system, manages foreign reserves and lends to sound banks in a crisis. Many also act as the government's banker and manage its debt auctions.

learn.h: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka
learn.body: Under the Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act of 2023, the bank's primary objective is domestic price stability and its secondary objective is financial system stability. A Monetary Policy Board sets policy under a flexible inflation targeting framework, aiming for CCPI inflation of around 5%. The Act also stops the bank from financing the government's budget.

India's Monetary Policy Committee has six members, three from the Reserve Bank and three external, and meets about six times a year. It targets CPI inflation of 4% within a band of 2% to 6%, and its main tool is the policy repo rate.

The Fed has a dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices, which it defines as 2% inflation on the PCE measure. Its Federal Open Market Committee sets a target range for the federal funds rate at eight scheduled meetings a year. Because the dollar is the world's main currency, Fed decisions move markets everywhere.

The policy rate is the main tool: in Sri Lanka, the overnight policy rate (OPR) introduced in November 2024. Standing facilities let banks deposit or borrow overnight at rates around it. Open market operations add or drain money. Reserve requirements, foreign exchange intervention and, in deep crises, large purchases of bonds (quantitative easing) are other tools.

Governments facing elections are tempted to keep rates low or to print money to fund spending, which leads to inflation. Giving central banks independence, a clear target and accountability for meeting it helps them make unpopular but necessary decisions. Research and experience across many countries link independence with lower inflation.

Central banks publish decisions, statements and reports on a schedule. Forward guidance, hints about future policy, shapes expectations and moves market rates before any change happens. Clear communication makes policy work faster and with fewer surprises.

en.title: Interest rates in everyday life
objectives: Explain how the policy rate reaches deposit and loan rates
Calculate real rates, effective annual rates and loan instalments
Weigh fixed against floating rates and local against foreign-currency loans

learn.h: From policy rate to your bank
learn.body: When the central bank changes its policy rate, overnight interbank rates move first, then Treasury bill yields, then banks' deposit and lending rates. The pass-through takes weeks for some rates and months for others, and is rarely one for one.

In Sri Lanka, the average weighted prime lending rate (AWPR), published weekly, shows what banks charge their best corporate customers. Average deposit rates and Treasury bill yields are other benchmarks. Many floating-rate loans are priced as a benchmark plus a margin.

The nominal rate is the rate on the contract. The real rate is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation, and it is what matters for your purchasing power. A 10% deposit when inflation is 12% loses value in real terms; a 10% deposit when inflation is 3% gains.

Rates quoted per month compound. A credit card charging 2% a month costs about 26.8% a year, not 24%, because interest is charged on interest. Always compare loans using the effective annual rate and all fees.

Most personal and housing loans are repaid in equal monthly instalments. Early instalments are mostly interest; later ones mostly repay the loan. A longer term lowers the instalment but raises the total interest paid.

A fixed rate stays the same for the term, which gives certainty but can be higher at the start. A floating rate moves with a benchmark, so instalments can rise sharply, as Sri Lankan borrowers found in 2022 when rates jumped. Match the choice to how much risk your budget can absorb.

Dollar loans often carry lower rates than rupee loans, but if your income is in rupees and the rupee falls, the debt grows in rupee terms. Many firms and countries, including Sri Lanka, have found that cheap foreign-currency debt became very expensive after a devaluation.

en.title: Sri Lanka's 2022 inflation surge
objectives: Explain the causes of Sri Lanka's 2022 inflation surge
Describe how monetary and fiscal policy brought inflation down
Compare Sri Lanka's experience with other high-inflation episodes

learn.body: Large tax cuts in late 2019 reduced government revenue sharply. When COVID-19 struck in 2020, the Central Bank cut policy rates to record lows and financed much of the budget deficit by buying Treasury bills, adding large amounts of new money. Foreign reserves fell as tourism collapsed and debt payments continued.

Through 2021 and into early 2022, the rupee was held near Rs 200 to the dollar while reserves ran down. Shortages of imported goods grew. In 2021 a sudden ban on chemical fertiliser imports cut harvests, pushing up food prices and import needs.

In March 2022 the rupee was allowed to float and fell to around Rs 360 to the dollar within weeks. At the same time, Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed up world prices of fuel, wheat and fertiliser. Import costs in rupees soared.

Colombo CCPI inflation peaked at 69.8% year on year in September 2022, and food inflation at about 95%. Households cut meals, and poverty rose sharply. Fuel queues, power cuts and medicine shortages made 2022 one of the hardest years in the country's history.

In April 2022 the Central Bank raised its policy rates by 7 percentage points in one move, and raised them again in July. The government raised VAT and income taxes, and moved fuel and electricity prices towards cost. Money financing of the budget was stopped, and an IMF programme followed in 2023.

Inflation fell faster than many expected: below 10% by mid-2023 as the rupee stabilised, import prices eased, harvests recovered and tight policy cooled demand. In late 2024 prices even fell year on year for some months, helped by cuts in electricity and fuel prices. Policy rates were then lowered step by step.

High inflation hit several economies at the same time. Turkey's inflation passed 80% in late 2022, Ghana's exceeded 50%, Pakistan's reached about 38% in 2023, and Argentina's passed 200% at the end of 2023. The common threads were weak public finances, money-financed deficits, falling currencies and lost confidence.

en.title: Week 2 review, test and project
summary: Money works because people trust it; it must serve as a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.
Banks create most money by lending; capital, liquidity rules and deposit insurance keep the system stable.
Inflation is measured with weighted price indices; food weighs heavily in South Asia, and inflation redistributes between groups.
Central banks such as the CBSL, the RBI and the Fed use policy rates and other tools to meet clear targets.
Policy rates pass through to deposits, loans and instalments; real rates and currency risk matter for every borrower and saver.
Sri Lanka's 2022 inflation surge came from money-financed deficits, a delayed currency adjustment and global shocks, and was reversed by tight policy and reform.

en.title: Why governments tax and spend
objectives: Explain why markets alone under-provide some goods
Describe the main types of tax and the principles of a good tax system
Compare how much governments tax and spend around the world

learn.body: Some goods are non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people cannot easily be stopped from using them): national defence, street lighting, flood protection. Private firms cannot charge for them, so markets provide too little. Governments step in and pay for them through taxes.

An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside a transaction. Pollution from a factory harms neighbours; vaccination protects people who are not vaccinated. Governments use taxes, subsidies and rules so that prices reflect these wider effects.

Education and health care benefit society beyond the individual, and people may under-use them if they must pay full cost. Sri Lanka's free education and health care since the 1940s are examples of governments providing merit goods. Governments also redistribute income through welfare and pensions.

In a recession, governments can cut taxes or raise spending to support demand; in a boom they can do the opposite. Automatic stabilisers, such as tax revenue that falls when incomes fall, work without new decisions. Using this role well needs room in the budget, which heavily indebted countries often lack.

Direct taxes fall on income and profits: personal income tax and corporate tax. Indirect taxes fall on spending: VAT, excise duties on fuel, alcohol and tobacco, and customs duties. A progressive tax takes a larger share from higher incomes; a regressive one takes a larger share from lower incomes.

learn.h: What makes a good tax system
learn.body: Economists look for efficiency (not distorting decisions more than needed), fairness (people in similar situations pay similar amounts, and those who can pay more do), simplicity and a broad base with few exemptions. Many exemptions and holidays make a system complex and leak revenue.

OECD countries collect on average about a third of GDP in taxes and social contributions. Most South Asian governments collect far less, and Sri Lanka's tax revenue fell to among the lowest shares in the world after the 2019 tax cuts. Raising it was a central part of the reforms after 2022.

en.title: Reading a national budget
objectives: Find revenue, spending, the deficit and its financing in a budget
Tell recurrent from capital spending
Compare budget calendars and processes in Sri Lanka, India and the US

learn.body: A national budget is the government's plan for revenue and spending for the coming fiscal year, and the law that authorises the spending. In Sri Lanka the Finance Minister presents the budget speech, usually in November, and Parliament passes an Appropriation Act. The fiscal year is the calendar year.

Revenue comes from taxes (income, VAT, excise, customs), non-tax revenue (fees, dividends from state enterprises, central bank profits) and grants. A budget states the expected amount for each source; the actual outcome can differ a lot if growth or collection disappoints.

Recurrent spending pays for things used up within the year: salaries, pensions, welfare, interest and running costs. Capital spending creates assets that last: roads, schools, power plants, water systems. Capital spending is often cut first when money is short, which can harm future growth.

The overall balance is total revenue minus total spending. The primary balance leaves out interest payments and shows whether current policy is adding to debt. The revenue balance (revenue minus recurrent spending) shows whether the government borrows even to pay for day-to-day costs.

A deficit must be financed: by borrowing at home (Treasury bills and bonds, bank loans), by borrowing abroad (bonds, loans from other governments and institutions), or, in the past, by central bank credit. Each has costs and risks, especially foreign-currency borrowing.

Good budgets are realistic, published in full, debated in parliament and reported on during the year. Sri Lanka's Public Financial Management Act of 2024 introduced fiscal rules and stronger reporting. India presents its budget on 1 February for a fiscal year from April to March; in the US, Congress passes appropriations for a fiscal year that starts in October.

Budget speeches highlight new spending and relief. The numbers that matter are often in the annexes: the revenue forecast and its assumptions, the primary balance, interest costs and the borrowing plan. Ask whether revenue assumptions are realistic and whether last year's targets were met.

en.title: Deficits and public debt
objectives: Tell deficits from debt and calculate debt ratios
Explain how interest rates and growth drive debt over time
Compare debt risks in Sri Lanka, Japan, India and the US

learn.body: The deficit is the gap between spending and revenue in one year, a flow. Public debt is the total stock of past borrowing still owed. Each year's deficit adds to the debt. Debt is usually measured as a share of GDP, because a larger economy can carry more debt.

Domestic debt is owed mostly to local banks, pension funds such as the EPF, and the central bank. External debt is owed to foreign governments, institutions such as the World Bank and ADB, and international bondholders. Debt in foreign currency is riskier, because it can only be repaid with dollars the country earns or borrows.

The debt ratio rises when the interest rate on debt is higher than the economy's growth rate, unless the government runs a primary surplus. If interest is 10% and nominal growth 6%, debt grows faster than the economy without a surplus to offset it. This is the logic of debt sustainability analysis.

High debt with high interest rates means a large share of revenue goes to interest, leaving less for schools, hospitals and roads. In Sri Lanka, interest payments took more than half of government revenue in recent years, one of the highest shares in the world.

Japan's public debt is over twice its GDP, yet it borrows cheaply because most debt is in yen, held at home, and Japan has a large pool of savings. The US borrows in the world's reserve currency. Countries that borrow in other people's currencies, with low revenue and reserves, can hit trouble at much lower debt levels.

Warning signs include rising debt with weak growth, a growing share of short-term or foreign-currency debt, low reserves, rising bond yields and difficulty rolling over maturing debt. Credit rating downgrades often follow and make borrowing harder.

Countries reduce debt ratios through primary surpluses, faster growth, lower interest rates, moderate inflation and, in a crisis, restructuring. Sri Lanka's IMF programme targets public debt below 95% of GDP by 2032, combining a primary surplus with debt relief.

en.title: State-owned enterprises
objectives: Explain why governments own businesses
Show how losses at state enterprises reach the budget and the banks
Compare reform options used in Sri Lanka, India, Singapore and China

learn.body: Governments own enterprises to provide services markets may not supply well, such as electricity grids and water, to control strategic sectors, or for historical and political reasons. Sri Lanka has several hundred state-owned enterprises, from the Ceylon Electricity Board and the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation to SriLankan Airlines and state banks.

learn.h: When prices are kept below cost
learn.body: If an enterprise must sell below cost, for example fuel or electricity at prices fixed for political reasons, it makes losses. It then borrows, often from state banks with government guarantees, and the losses eventually land on taxpayers. Before 2022, the CEB and CPC built up very large losses this way.

Losses at state enterprises do not always show in the budget at first. They appear as guarantees, unpaid bills and loans from state banks. When the government finally takes over the debt, as it did for some of SriLankan Airlines' borrowing, public debt jumps. These are called contingent liabilities.

From 2022, Sri Lanka moved fuel and electricity towards cost-reflective pricing, with formulas that pass on cost changes. This cut losses sharply but raised bills for households, which is why targeted support for the poorest matters alongside it.

Well-run state enterprises have professional boards, clear commercial goals, published accounts and separate funding for any social tasks the government wants them to do. Political appointments, unclear goals and no accountability are common causes of failure.

Options include restructuring and better governance, bringing enterprises under a holding company, opening sectors to private competition, public-private partnerships, partial listing on the stock exchange and full privatisation. India sold Air India to the Tata group in 2022 after years of losses.

Singapore's Temasek holds stakes in companies run on commercial lines with independent boards. China's state enterprises dominate key sectors but face repeated reform drives to improve efficiency. Each model reflects how much the state wants to control, and how well it can hold managers to account.

en.title: The IMF and the World Bank
objectives: Explain how the IMF lends and what conditions it sets
Explain how the World Bank and the ADB finance development
Weigh the benefits and criticisms of IMF programmes

learn.body: The International Monetary Fund has 191 member countries. Members pay in quotas, which set their votes and how much they can borrow. The IMF monitors every member through annual Article IV reports and lends when a country cannot pay for essential imports or service its debts.

A country agrees a programme with targets, called conditionality: for example a primary surplus, a minimum level of reserves, a ceiling on central bank lending to the government, or reforms to tax and state enterprises. Money is released in instalments after each review, usually every six months.

A Stand-By Arrangement supports short-term problems. The Extended Fund Facility supports longer, deeper reforms and is what Sri Lanka received in 2023. Special funds offer cheaper terms to low-income countries. The IMF's money also unlocks other lenders, who often wait for its approval.

The World Bank finances long-term development: roads, power, water, schools, health systems and social protection. Its IBRD arm lends to middle-income countries on near-market terms; its IDA arm gives very cheap loans and grants to the poorest. It also provides research and policy advice.

The ADB, based in Manila, plays a similar role across Asia and the Pacific. It is one of Sri Lanka's largest lenders for infrastructure and supported budget reforms after 2022. Japan and the United States are its largest shareholders.

Critics say IMF programmes can demand cuts that hurt the poor, move too fast, or ignore local conditions; the Asian crisis programmes of 1997 drew strong criticism. Newer programmes include social spending floors, as Sri Lanka's does, and pay more attention to governance and poverty.

learn.h: Why countries still turn to the IMF
learn.body: When a country runs out of reserves, the alternatives are severe import cuts or disorderly default. The IMF provides money, a policy framework and a signal of credibility. Its programmes work best when the government owns the reforms and they keep public support.

en.title: Sri Lanka's debt crisis and restructuring
objectives: Describe the timeline of Sri Lanka's default and restructuring
Explain how domestic and external restructurings work
Compare Sri Lanka's restructuring with Ghana's and Zambia's

learn.body: On 12 April 2022, with reserves nearly exhausted, Sri Lanka announced it would suspend payments on most of its external debt pending restructuring. It was the first sovereign default in the country's history. Without the dollars to pay, the alternative was to keep paying creditors while fuel and medicines ran out.

Debt was over 100% of GDP, much of it in foreign currency, interest took over half of revenue and reserves were near zero. The IMF judged the debt unsustainable, so it could only lend if creditors agreed to restructure enough to bring debt back to safe levels: public debt below 95% of GDP by 2032 and lower foreign-currency debt service.

In mid-2023 Sri Lanka restructured part of its domestic debt. Treasury bonds held by superannuation funds such as the EPF were exchanged for new bonds with lower interest, and the Central Bank's holdings of Treasury bills were converted into longer bonds. Bank deposits were protected to avoid a banking crisis.

Bilateral lenders negotiated through an Official Creditor Committee co-chaired by Japan, India and France, while China's Export-Import Bank negotiated separately. Agreements extended maturities and lowered interest, giving Sri Lanka years of lower payments. Final deals were signed in 2024.

Private holders of international sovereign bonds agreed to exchange old bonds for new ones in late 2024. The new bonds have a lower face value and interest, and some are linked to future economic performance, paying more if GDP grows faster than expected. Credit ratings were raised after the exchange.

Ghana defaulted on most external debt in December 2022 and restructured under the G20 Common Framework. Zambia, which defaulted in 2020, took years to reach agreements, showing how slow coordination between Chinese, Western and private creditors can be. Sri Lanka, as a middle-income country, negotiated outside the Common Framework but along similar lines.

Restructuring buys time, but it does not fix the causes. Sri Lanka must keep a primary surplus, raise exports and revenue, and avoid building up foreign-currency debt again. Debt payments will rise again later in the decade, so reforms have to last.

en.title: Trade and comparative advantage
objectives: Explain comparative advantage and the gains from trade
Calculate opportunity costs to find who should specialise
Explain who gains and who loses from tariffs

learn.body: Countries trade for the same reason people do: specialising in what you do relatively well and buying the rest makes everyone better off. Sri Lanka grows tea and sews garments efficiently; buying machinery, fuel and medicines from countries that make them cheaply costs less than making them at home.

A country has an absolute advantage if it can produce more of a good with the same resources. It has a comparative advantage if its opportunity cost of producing the good is lower. David Ricardo showed in 1817 that trade benefits both sides even if one country is better at producing everything, as long as opportunity costs differ.

When each country specialises in its comparative advantage and trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond their own production possibilities frontier. Trade also brings competition, new technology and a wider choice of goods, which raise productivity.

Trade creates winners and losers within a country. Workers and firms in industries that face new imports can lose jobs and income, even when the country as a whole gains. Good policy helps people move to new jobs through training, support and a strong economy, rather than blocking trade.

A tariff is a tax on imports. It raises prices for consumers, protects local producers and raises revenue, but it reduces trade and usually lowers national income overall. Sri Lanka has used para-tariffs, extra levies on top of customs duties, which international lenders have urged it to phase out.

Sri Lanka's closed economy in the early 1970s brought shortages and slow growth; opening up from 1977 brought garment factories and faster growth. East Asian economies such as South Korea and Vietnam grew rapidly by exporting manufactures to world markets.

learn.h: Trade in a world of tariffs
learn.body: Trade rules are set through the WTO and through free trade agreements. In 2025 the United States raised tariffs on imports from many countries, including Sri Lanka, whose largest single export market for apparel is the US. Small exporters must spread their markets and products to reduce such risks.

en.title: Exports, tourism and remittances
objectives: Describe Sri Lanka's main sources of foreign currency
Calculate shares, growth rates and the current account
Explain the risks of depending on a few earners

learn.body: Sri Lanka earns foreign currency from goods exports (apparel, tea, rubber products, coconut and spices), services (tourism, IT and business services, shipping and logistics) and workers' remittances. It spends foreign currency on imports of fuel, food, medicines, machinery and inputs for factories, and on debt service.

Apparel makes up the largest share of merchandise exports, with tea second. The United States and the European Union are the largest markets. Export earnings have grown slowly compared with GDP for two decades, which is a key reason the country ran short of dollars.

Tourist arrivals reached a record of about 2.3 million in 2018, collapsed after the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks and COVID-19, and recovered to about 2 million in 2024. Tourism brings dollars quickly and creates jobs in many regions, but it is very sensitive to security, health scares and travel advisories.

Money sent home by Sri Lankans working abroad, mainly in the Gulf, reached record levels of around 6.5 billion dollars in 2024. Remittances are often the largest single source of foreign currency, larger than tea and tourism combined, and they support household spending across the country.

The current account adds the trade balance in goods, the balance on services, net primary income (such as interest and profits paid abroad) and net transfers such as remittances. A deficit must be financed by borrowing or investment from abroad; a surplus adds to reserves or repays debt.

Depending on a few products, markets or earners is risky. A shock to apparel demand, a tourism collapse or a fall in Gulf jobs can quickly cut dollar inflows. Countries that grew fast, such as Vietnam, built a much wider base of manufactured exports.

IT and business process services, logistics around Colombo port and higher-value food and spice products are growing. India shows how services exports can grow into a major earner. Raising skills, connectivity and investment rules will decide how far Sri Lanka can follow.

en.title: Exchange rates for beginners
objectives: Explain how supply and demand for dollars set the exchange rate
Compare floating, managed and fixed exchange rate regimes
Explain the effects of depreciation on prices, exporters and debt

learn.body: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. USD/LKR 300 means a dollar costs 300 rupees. Like other prices, it moves with supply and demand: dollars supplied by exporters, tourists, migrant workers and foreign investors, and dollars demanded by importers, borrowers repaying debt and people sending money abroad.

When more rupees are needed to buy a dollar, the rupee has depreciated; when fewer are needed, it has appreciated. Depreciation makes imports more expensive and exports cheaper for foreign buyers. It raises inflation, especially in import-heavy economies, and increases the rupee cost of foreign-currency debt.

Under a floating rate, the market sets the price and the central bank intervenes rarely. Under a fixed or pegged rate, the central bank buys or sells currency to hold a set price. Many emerging economies run a managed float, letting the rate move while smoothing sharp swings.

learn.h: Examples from Asia and the Gulf
learn.body: Sri Lanka and India run managed floats. China manages the yuan within a band around a daily reference rate. Hong Kong pegs its dollar in a narrow band around 7.8 to the US dollar, and Saudi Arabia pegs the riyal at 3.75. A peg needs large reserves to defend it.

learn.h: The cost of holding a rate
learn.body: Holding a rate that is out of line with the economy drains reserves, because the central bank must sell dollars to keep the rupee strong. Sri Lanka did this through 2021 and into 2022; when reserves ran out, the rupee fell sharply all at once. Gradual adjustment is usually less damaging.

The real exchange rate adjusts for inflation in each country. If the rupee falls 10% but Sri Lankan prices rise 10% more than prices abroad, competitiveness is unchanged. What matters for exporters is the real rate, not just the number on the board.

Foreign reserves are the central bank's holdings of foreign currency and gold. They pay for imports in emergencies and let the bank smooth the exchange rate. A common rule of thumb is reserves covering at least three months of imports; Sri Lanka's fell far below that in 2022.

en.title: South Asia's economies
objectives: Compare the size, income and structure of South Asian economies
Use GDP per capita and growth rates to compare countries
Explain why trade within South Asia is low

learn.body: South Asia covers India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives and Afghanistan. It is home to about a quarter of the world's people but produces a much smaller share of world GDP. India alone accounts for roughly four fifths of the region's output.

Sri Lanka and the Maldives have the highest GDP per capita in South Asia (excluding small Bhutan in some years), around 4,000 dollars or more for Sri Lanka. India is around 2,500 dollars, Bangladesh similar, Pakistan and Nepal lower. Income per person, not total GDP, is the better guide to living standards.

Bangladesh grew fast on garment exports and social progress, especially for women. India's growth leaned on services such as IT, then manufacturing and infrastructure. Pakistan and Sri Lanka have suffered repeated balance of payments crises and IMF programmes. The Maldives depends heavily on tourism.

Sri Lanka has long had higher life expectancy, literacy and school enrolment than its neighbours, thanks to free education and health care since the mid-20th century. That human capital is an advantage, though skilled emigration has increased since the 2022 crisis.

Trade within South Asia is only about 5% of the region's total trade, compared with around 25% within ASEAN. High tariffs, poor transport links, border delays and political tension, especially between India and Pakistan, hold it back. SAFTA, the South Asian Free Trade Area, has had limited impact.

India is one of Sri Lanka's largest sources of imports and tourists. The Indo-Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement took effect in 2000. In the 2022 crisis India gave about 4 billion dollars in credit lines and currency support. Proposals for energy grids, ports and digital payments links continue.

When comparing countries, use the same source and year, convert at market exchange rates or at purchasing power parity (PPP), and look at per-person figures. PPP adjusts for lower prices in poorer countries and makes living standards more comparable.

en.title: China, India and the global economy
objectives: Describe the rise of China and India and their growth models
Explain how they affect small economies such as Sri Lanka
Compare shares of world GDP and trade

learn.body: China and India together have over a third of the world's population. China is the world's second-largest economy at market exchange rates and the largest in purchasing power terms. India became the fifth-largest economy in the mid-2020s and is among the fastest-growing large economies.

From 1978, China opened to foreign investment and trade, moved farmers into factories and invested heavily in infrastructure. Growth near 10% a year for three decades lifted around 800 million people out of extreme poverty. Growth has slowed to around 5% as the population ages and property debt weighs.

India's reforms began in 1991 after a balance of payments crisis. Services such as IT and business outsourcing led growth, followed by manufacturing, roads, digital payments (UPI) and identity systems. India has a young, growing workforce, but needs to create many more good jobs.

learn.h: The world's factory and the world's back office
learn.body: China dominates manufacturing in electronics, machinery, solar panels and batteries, and is the largest trading partner of many countries. India is a major exporter of software and business services and of medicines. Both are big buyers of oil, metals and food, so their growth moves commodity prices.

learn.h: What it means for Sri Lanka
learn.body: China and India are Sri Lanka's two largest sources of imports. China financed major projects such as Hambantota port and Port City Colombo and became a large official creditor. India is a major source of tourists and investment. Sri Lanka balances relations with both while seeking trade, investment and debt relief.

Big neighbours bring markets, investment and supply chains, but also competition for local producers and geopolitical pressure. Rivalry between major powers in the Indian Ocean raises the strategic value of Sri Lanka's location, which can bring investment but also complicate policy.

In 1990 China and India together produced under 5% of world GDP at market rates; today it is roughly a quarter. The world's economic centre of gravity has moved towards Asia, which is why Asian growth now matters as much to Sri Lanka as growth in Europe or the US.

en.title: Globalisation and supply chains
objectives: Explain globalisation and global value chains
Analyse how supply chain shocks spread across countries
Identify how Sri Lanka can move into higher-value activities

learn.body: Globalisation is the growing connection of economies through trade, investment, finance, migration, information and ideas. Cheaper shipping (the container), the internet and lower trade barriers made it possible to produce goods across many countries.

A smartphone or a shirt is designed in one country, uses parts from several others, is assembled in another and sold worldwide. Each step adds value. Today a large share of world trade is in parts and components moving within these global value chains.

Most value is added at the ends of the chain: research, design and branding at one end, marketing, logistics and service at the other. Basic assembly in the middle earns least. Countries develop by moving towards the high-value ends, as Taiwan and South Korea did in electronics.

Sri Lankan firms such as MAS Holdings and Brandix started as sewing contractors and moved into design, fabric development, technical materials and ethical production for global brands. That upgrading kept them competitive against lower-wage rivals.

Long, lean supply chains are efficient but fragile. COVID-19 lockdowns, container shortages, the 2021 Suez Canal blockage and Red Sea shipping attacks from 2023 raised freight costs and delays worldwide. A shock in one place spreads quickly through prices and shortages elsewhere.

Firms now spread production across countries ('China plus one'), keep more stock and move some production closer to home or to friendly countries. This shift creates openings for countries such as Vietnam, India and potentially Sri Lanka, if they offer skills, reliable power and stable policy.

Globalisation helped lift billions out of poverty, mainly in Asia, but some workers in rich countries lost jobs and inequality rose in places. Rising tariffs and rivalry between major powers mean the coming decades may bring slower, more regional globalisation.

en.title: Budgeting
objectives: Explain what a budget is and why it matters
Sort spending into needs, wants and savings
Build a simple monthly budget and find a surplus or deficit

learn.body: A budget is a plan for your money: what comes in, where it goes and what is left. It is not about spending less on everything; it is about spending on purpose. People and families who budget save more, borrow less and handle shocks better, whatever their income.

Start with take-home pay: salary after EPF contributions and any tax (PAYE, called APIT in Sri Lanka). Add regular extra income such as rent, a side business or money sent by family abroad. Use what you reliably receive, not what you hope to earn; irregular income is best averaged over several months.

Fixed costs are about the same every month: rent or housing loan, school fees, insurance, loan instalments. Variable costs change: food, electricity, fuel, mobile data, eating out. Most savings come from variable spending, because fixed costs are hard to change quickly.

Needs are what you must pay to live and work: housing, basic food, utilities, transport, health. Wants are pleasant but optional: eating out, new phones, subscriptions. A common guide is the 50/30/20 rule: 50% of take-home pay on needs, 30% on wants and 20% on saving or repaying debt. Where living costs are high, the split may be closer to 60/20/20; the habit matters more than the exact numbers.

Move your savings out on payday, before spending, with a standing order to a separate account. What you do not see you do not spend. Saving whatever is left at the end of the month rarely works, because there is usually nothing left.

A budget only works if you compare it with what you actually spend. Track for one month using a notebook, a spreadsheet or your bank's app. Most people find a few 'leaks', small regular spends such as snacks, delivery fees or unused subscriptions, that add up to a large amount over a year.

If income exceeds spending, you have a surplus to save or invest. If spending exceeds income, you have a deficit, which must be covered by savings or borrowing. A household running a deficit month after month is heading for trouble, just as a government running large deficits is.

en.title: Saving and the emergency fund
objectives: Explain why saving matters and set savings goals
Size an emergency fund and choose where to keep it
Calculate how long it takes to reach a savings goal

learn.body: Saving turns today's income into future choices: a cushion for emergencies, money for big goals such as a home, education or a wedding, and eventually investments that grow. Saving also lowers stress and reduces the need to borrow at high interest.

An emergency fund is money set aside only for unexpected events: losing a job, illness, urgent repairs or helping family. A common guide is three to six months of essential spending. People with irregular income, one earner in the family or a less secure job should aim for the higher end.

Emergency money must be safe and easy to reach quickly. A savings account or a short-term fixed deposit at a licensed bank works well. It should not be in shares, property, gold jewellery you would hate to sell, or money lent to friends, because you may not get it back when you need it.

Good savings goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. 'Save more' is vague; 'save Rs 600,000 for a motorbike in 24 months, Rs 25,000 a month' is a plan. Divide the goal by the months available to find the monthly amount.

Short-term goals (under a year) belong in savings accounts. Medium-term goals (one to five years) can use fixed deposits or Treasury bills. Long-term goals such as retirement can take more risk for higher returns, which later programmes cover. Matching the product to the time horizon is a key rule of personal finance.

Habits beat willpower. Set up a standing order on payday, save windfalls such as bonuses and festival allowances, and round up purchases into savings if your bank offers it. Increasing savings by a small amount each time your pay rises makes saving painless.

Household saving habits differ: Chinese and Indian households save a large share of income, partly because of weaker social safety nets, while US households save much less. In Sri Lanka, many families save through gold, chit funds (seettu) and fixed deposits. Seettu builds discipline but carries the risk that the organiser or a member defaults.

en.title: Bank accounts and cards
objectives: Compare current, savings and fixed deposit accounts
Explain the difference between debit and credit cards
Calculate the cost of credit card interest and fees

learn.body: A savings account holds money safely, pays some interest and lets you withdraw when needed. Rates are usually low and change with market rates. Many banks offer special accounts for children, women, seniors and migrant workers' families, sometimes with higher rates or benefits.

A current account is designed for frequent payments, usually by businesses. It comes with a cheque book, may offer an overdraft, and normally pays no interest. Writing a cheque without enough money in the account is a serious offence in Sri Lanka and damages your credit record.

A fixed deposit (FD) locks money for a set term, from one month to five years, at a fixed rate that is higher than on savings accounts. Withdrawing early usually means a lower rate or a penalty. Interest can be paid monthly or at maturity; tax is withheld on interest earned.

A debit card spends money already in your account, at shops, online and at ATMs. It is convenient and you cannot spend more than you have, unless an overdraft is attached. Watch for fees on ATM withdrawals at other banks and on foreign transactions.

A credit card lets you borrow up to a limit and repay later. If you pay the full balance by the due date, there is usually no interest, which makes cards useful for convenience and building a credit record. If you pay only the minimum, the rest attracts high interest, often 2% to 3% a month, plus late fees.

The minimum payment is often only a small percentage of the balance. Paying just the minimum keeps the account in good standing but repays debt very slowly, and the interest can exceed the original purchase. Treat a credit card as a payment tool, not as extra income.

Compare interest rates, fees, minimum balances, ATM networks, mobile app quality and customer service. In Sri Lanka, licensed commercial banks and licensed specialised banks are regulated by the Central Bank. Globally, the same basics apply: the cheapest account is the one whose fees you avoid by using it the way it is designed.

en.title: How interest works
objectives: Explain interest as the price of money
Calculate simple interest and compare rates
Explain why rates differ between products and over time

learn.body: Interest is the price of using someone else's money for a time. When you deposit money, the bank pays you interest for using it. When you borrow, you pay interest to the lender. The rate is usually quoted per year as a percentage of the amount, called the principal.

Simple interest is paid only on the original principal: interest = principal × rate × time. Rs 100,000 at 10% a year for 3 years earns 100,000 × 0.10 × 3 = Rs 30,000. Next week covers compound interest, where interest also earns interest.

Lenders charge for three things: giving up the use of their money now, the risk that the borrower will not repay, and inflation reducing what the money will buy. Riskier borrowers and longer loans usually pay higher rates.

Banks pay depositors a lower rate than they charge borrowers. The difference, the interest spread, covers their costs, bad loans and profit. If a bank pays 8% on deposits and lends at 13%, its spread is 5 percentage points.

The central bank sets a policy rate, the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) in Sri Lanka, which influences what banks pay and charge. When it raises rates to fight inflation, deposit and loan rates tend to rise; when it cuts, they tend to fall. In 2022 Sri Lankan rates rose above 25%; they fell back to single digits by 2024.

A fixed rate stays the same for the term. A floating (variable) rate moves with a benchmark, such as AWPR in Sri Lanka or SOFR in the US, plus a margin. Floating rates are cheaper when rates fall and more expensive when they rise, so borrowers take on rate risk.

Always check whether a rate is per year or per month, simple or compound, and fixed or floating. A flat rate on a vehicle loan, charged on the original amount for the whole term, costs far more than the same reducing-balance rate. Week 2 shows how to compare them.

en.title: Borrowing and credit reports (CRIB)
objectives: Distinguish good and bad uses of debt
Explain what a CRIB report and credit score show
Calculate a debt-service ratio and judge affordability

learn.body: Borrowing lets you use future income today. It can make sense for things that last or raise your income, such as a home, education or tools for a business, at a cost you can afford. It is risky for things that lose value quickly or for everyday spending, because you keep paying long after the benefit is gone.

Common loans include personal loans, housing loans, vehicle leasing, gold loans (pawning), credit cards and overdrafts. Secured loans are backed by an asset that the lender can take if you do not repay, such as a house, vehicle or gold, and usually cost less. Unsecured loans cost more.

Lenders look at the debt-service ratio: monthly loan repayments divided by monthly income. Many lenders want it below 40%. Leave room for emergencies and rate rises; a loan that only just fits today can become a burden if income falls or rates rise.

The Credit Information Bureau of Sri Lanka (CRIB) collects credit data from banks and finance companies on every borrower: loans, cards, limits, repayments and arrears. Lenders check your CRIB report before lending. You can request your own report and CRIB Score, and should check it for errors.

Credit scores summarise your record as a number. In India, CIBIL scores range from 300 to 900; in the United States, FICO scores range from 300 to 850. Higher scores mean lower risk and usually better rates. Paying on time, keeping card balances low and not applying for too much credit at once all help.

Missing payments leads to late fees, higher interest and a poor credit record that can last for years. Serious default can lead to the lender taking secured assets or legal action. If you struggle, talk to the lender early: rescheduling is usually better than default for both sides.

Be wary of unlicensed money lenders and loan apps offering instant cash. They may charge very high rates, use aggressive collection, or misuse your phone data. In Sri Lanka, rural microfinance debt became a serious problem in the late 2010s. Borrow only from institutions licensed or registered with the Central Bank.

en.title: Insurance basics
objectives: Explain how insurance pools risk
Describe the main types of insurance and key terms
Decide which risks to insure and which to cover yourself

learn.body: Insurance lets many people share the cost of rare but expensive events. Each pays a small, certain premium into a pool, and the few who suffer a loss are paid from it. It works because insurers can predict how many claims a large group will make, even though no one knows who will claim.

The premium is what you pay for cover. The sum insured is the most the policy will pay. The excess (or deductible) is the part of each claim you pay yourself. Exclusions are events the policy does not cover. The policy document sets out all of these; read it before signing.

Life insurance pays your family if you die during the cover period. Term insurance gives pure protection for a set number of years and is cheap. Endowment and whole-life policies combine protection with savings, cost much more, and often give modest returns. People with dependants usually need term cover worth several years of income.

Sri Lanka's free public hospitals cover a great deal, but private treatment can be costly. Health insurance pays for hospital stays and sometimes outpatient care. Many employers provide group cover, and public servants have the Agrahara scheme. Check limits per illness and per year, waiting periods and pre-existing condition rules.

General insurance covers property and liability: motor, home, fire, travel and business cover. Third-party motor insurance is compulsory in Sri Lanka. Comprehensive motor cover also pays for damage to your own vehicle. Home and fire cover protect against fire, floods and theft.

Insure risks that would be very costly and that you cannot cover from savings: death of an earner, serious illness, major property loss and liability to others. Small, frequent costs, such as minor repairs, are often cheaper to pay yourself. A higher excess lowers premiums if you have an emergency fund.

Insurers in Sri Lanka are regulated by the Insurance Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka (IRCSL). Before buying, compare insurers' claim settlement records. Always disclose information truthfully, because false or missing disclosures can void a claim.

en.title: Simple and compound interest
objectives: Calculate compound interest over several periods
Explain how compounding frequency changes returns
Compare simple and compound growth over long periods

learn.body: With compound interest, each period's interest is added to the balance and earns interest itself. Rs 100,000 at 10% grows to Rs 110,000 after one year, then Rs 121,000 after two, because the second year's interest is paid on Rs 110,000. Simple interest would give only Rs 120,000.

Future value = present value × (1 + r)ⁿ, where r is the rate per period and n the number of periods. Rs 100,000 at 10% for 3 years becomes 100,000 × 1.1³ = Rs 133,100. A calculator or spreadsheet does the powers for you; the habit to build is setting up the formula correctly.

Interest can be added yearly, half-yearly, quarterly, monthly or daily. The more often it is added, the faster the balance grows. 12% a year compounded monthly means 1% a month, which gives 1.01¹² − 1 ≈ 12.68% over a year, more than 12%.

The advertised rate is the nominal rate. The effective annual rate (also called the annual equivalent rate, AER, or annual percentage yield, APY, in the US) shows what you really earn or pay over a year after compounding. Comparing effective rates puts different products on the same basis.

Compounding is slow at first and powerful later. Rs 100,000 at 10% grows to about Rs 259,000 in 10 years, Rs 673,000 in 20 years and Rs 1.74 million in 30 years. Starting to save early matters more than saving large amounts later.

Unpaid interest on credit cards and loans is added to the debt and also compounds. That is why a credit card balance at 2.5% a month can almost double in under three years if nothing is repaid. The same arithmetic that builds savings builds debt.

Compounding applies to anything that grows by a percentage: GDP, populations, prices and investment returns. Inflation compounds too, which is why prices that rise 'only' 6% a year are about 80% higher after ten years. You will use the same formula throughout finance and economics.

en.title: The rule of 72
objectives: Use the rule of 72 to estimate doubling times
Estimate the rate needed to double money in a given time
Apply the rule to inflation, debt and growth

learn.body: The rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double: divide 72 by the annual interest rate in percent. At 8%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. At 12%, about 6 years. It saves reaching for a calculator and helps you sense whether an offer is realistic.

Divide 72 by the number of years to find the rate needed to double. To double money in 6 years you need about 72 ÷ 6 = 12% a year. Anyone promising to double your money in 6 months is implying about 144% a year, which should raise immediate questions.

The rule is very close for rates between about 6% and 10%, and still useful from 2% to 20%. At 9%, it gives 8 years; the exact answer is 8.04 years. For continuous growth, economists often use 70 or 69 instead; you met the rule of 70 in Economics Foundation.

Each doubling builds on the last. Rs 1 million at 9% becomes about Rs 2 million in 8 years, Rs 4 million in 16 years and Rs 8 million in 24 years. That is the shape of compound growth: slow at first, then steep.

The rule also tells you how fast inflation halves purchasing power. At 6% inflation, prices double, and the value of cash halves, in about 12 years. At 3%, it takes about 24 years. During Sri Lanka's 2022 crisis, when inflation briefly exceeded 60%, prices could double in barely more than a year.
An unpaid debt at 24% a year doubles in about 3 years. A loan app charging 10% a month, about 120% a year, can double a debt in well under a year. The rule makes the danger of high rates easy to see.

An economy growing 7% a year doubles its output in about 10 years; one growing 3% takes about 24 years. That is why small differences in growth rates between countries such as India, Vietnam and Sri Lanka add up to large gaps in living standards over a generation.

en.title: Inflation and real returns
objectives: Distinguish nominal and real returns
Calculate real returns and lost purchasing power
Explain why savers can lose money even when earning interest

learn.body: The nominal return is the percentage your money grows in rupees. The real return is how much more you can actually buy, after inflation. If a fixed deposit pays 10% and prices rise 6%, your real return is about 4%.

The quick approximation is real ≈ nominal − inflation. The exact formula is real = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1. With 10% and 6%, that gives 1.10 ÷ 1.06 − 1 ≈ 3.77%. The quick version is fine at low rates; use the exact one when inflation is high.

When inflation is above the interest rate, the real return is negative: you have more rupees but can buy less. In 2022 Sri Lankan deposit rates rose above 20%, yet inflation reached about 70%, so savers lost a large part of their purchasing power.

Sri Lanka measures inflation with the Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI) and the National Consumer Price Index (NCPI). The Central Bank aims to keep inflation around 5%. India's central bank targets 4%, and the US Federal Reserve and many others target 2%.

Tax is usually charged on the nominal interest, not the real gain. If interest is 10%, tax takes a tenth of it and inflation is 6%, the after-tax return is 9% and the real after-tax return is only about 3%. In high-inflation years tax can turn a small real gain into a loss.

Over long periods, assets such as shares, property and gold have tended to keep up with or beat inflation, while cash has not, but they carry more risk and can fall sharply in the short run. Some governments issue inflation-linked bonds, such as US TIPS. Week 4 and later programmes look at these choices.

People often think in nominal terms: a 10% pay rise feels good even if prices rose 12%. Economists call this money illusion. Training yourself to think in real terms, for wages, savings and prices, is one of the most useful habits in finance.

en.title: Present value in plain terms
objectives: Explain why money today is worth more than the same amount later
Calculate the present value of a future sum
Compare offers paid at different times

learn.h: A rupee today beats a rupee tomorrow
learn.body: Money you have today can be saved and earn interest, spent now, or kept safe from the risk of not being paid later. So Rs 100,000 today is worth more than Rs 100,000 in a year's time. This idea, the time value of money, is the foundation of all finance.

Present value turns a future amount into today's money by reversing compounding: present value = future value ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ. At 10%, Rs 110,000 in one year is worth 110,000 ÷ 1.10 = Rs 100,000 today. Moving money back in time is called discounting, and r is the discount rate.

The discount rate is the return you could earn elsewhere at similar risk, your opportunity cost. For a safe promise, a Treasury bill or fixed deposit rate is a sensible choice. For a riskier promise, use a higher rate, because uncertain money is worth less.

The discount factor 1 ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ shows what Rs 1 in the future is worth today. At 8%, Rs 1 in five years is worth about Rs 0.68 today; in twenty years, about Rs 0.21. The further away the money and the higher the rate, the less it is worth now.

To compare amounts paid at different times, bring them all to today's value. Rs 600,000 in two years versus Rs 500,000 now: at 10%, the future sum is worth 600,000 ÷ 1.21 ≈ Rs 495,868 today, so the money now is slightly better. At 8% the answer flips.

An annuity is a series of equal payments, such as a pension, rent or loan instalments. Its present value is the sum of each payment's present value. Spreadsheets do this with the PV function. Tomorrow's lesson uses the same idea to find loan instalments.

Banks use present value to price loans, investors to value bonds and shares, insurers to set premiums, governments to judge projects such as highways and power plants, and courts to calculate compensation. Learning it now makes later topics much easier.

en.title: Loans and monthly instalments
objectives: Explain how equal monthly instalments repay a loan
Calculate an instalment and the total interest paid
Compare flat and reducing-balance rates

learn.body: Most personal, vehicle and housing loans are repaid in equal monthly instalments (EMIs). Each payment covers that month's interest plus part of the principal. Early payments are mostly interest; later ones are mostly principal, because the balance and therefore the interest keep shrinking.

Instalment = P × r × (1 + r)ⁿ ÷ ((1 + r)ⁿ − 1), where P is the loan, r the monthly rate and n the number of months. A Rs 1 million loan at 12% a year (1% a month) over 12 months costs about Rs 88,849 a month. Spreadsheets use the PMT function to do this.

An amortisation schedule lists each payment's interest and principal and the balance left. In the first month of that Rs 1 million loan, interest is Rs 10,000 and Rs 78,849 repays principal. Ask your lender for the schedule; it shows exactly what you are paying for.

Stretching a loan over more years lowers the instalment but raises the total interest. A Rs 5 million housing loan at 12% costs about Rs 55,000 a month over 20 years, and the total paid is over Rs 13 million. Choose the shortest term you can comfortably afford.

Some vehicle loans and leases quote a flat rate, charged on the original amount for the whole term even as you repay. A 12% flat rate over three years costs about the same as a reducing-balance rate of over 21%. Always ask for the reducing-balance equivalent, sometimes shown as the effective or annual percentage rate.

Compare documentation fees, insurance required by the lender, valuation fees and penalties for paying early. Paying extra on the principal, when allowed without heavy penalties, can save a lot of interest because every rupee repaid stops earning interest for the lender.

With a floating-rate loan, the instalment or the term can change when rates move. A 3 percentage point rise on a large housing loan can add thousands of rupees a month. Before borrowing, check that you could still afford the instalment if rates rose.

en.title: Comparing deposits across banks
objectives: Compare deposit offers on an effective-rate basis
Weigh return against safety, access and fees
Build a simple comparison table

learn.body: Banks advertise rates in different ways: interest paid monthly, quarterly or at maturity, special rates for seniors, and promotional rates for new money. To compare fairly, convert each to an effective annual rate and use the same amount and term.

A deposit that pays interest monthly usually offers a slightly lower rate than one paying at maturity. If you reinvest the monthly interest, the effective rates can be similar. If you spend it, as many retirees do, the monthly option gives income but no compounding.

Longer terms often pay more but lock your money away. If rates are expected to fall, locking in a longer term can be good; if rates are expected to rise, shorter terms keep options open. Splitting money across several maturity dates, called laddering, balances the two.

A higher rate often means higher risk. Licensed commercial banks are generally safer than licensed finance companies, which in turn are safer than unregistered deposit-takers. Several finance companies in Sri Lanka have failed, and depositors waited years for partial repayment. Week 3 covers deposit insurance, which protects up to a limit.

Tax may be withheld from interest, and some accounts charge fees or require minimum balances. The figure that matters is the return you keep after tax and fees, and, as you learned on day 10, after inflation.

For money you will not need for a year or more, Treasury bills and bonds, covered in week 4, can pay similar or higher returns with government backing. Money market unit trusts are another option. Each has different risks, access and minimum amounts.

Put the options in a table: institution, licence type, product, amount, term, nominal rate, payment frequency, effective rate, fees, early withdrawal terms and deposit insurance cover. Writing it out makes the trade-offs clear and stops marketing from deciding for you.

en.title: How banks work
objectives: Read a simple bank balance sheet
Explain how banks earn money and what can go wrong
Calculate key bank ratios

learn.body: Banks take deposits from savers and lend to households, businesses and the government. They turn short-term, easy-to-withdraw deposits into longer-term loans, a job called maturity transformation. They also run payment systems, exchange currency and offer services such as trade finance and wealth management.

A bank's assets are what it owns or is owed: loans, government securities, cash and reserves at the central bank. Its liabilities are what it owes: mainly customer deposits and borrowings. Equity, the shareholders' capital, is assets minus liabilities. Your deposit is the bank's liability and your asset.

The main source of income is net interest income: interest earned on loans and securities minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings. Banks also earn fees and commissions on cards, remittances, trade services and foreign exchange. From this they pay staff, technology, taxes and bad-loan losses.

Some borrowers do not repay. Loans that are seriously overdue are called non-performing loans (NPLs); in Sri Lanka's reporting, the worst category is Stage 3 loans. Banks set aside provisions for expected losses. After the 2022 crisis, bad loans rose sharply as businesses and households struggled with high rates and falling incomes.

Banks keep only part of deposits as cash and liquid assets. If too many depositors try to withdraw at once, even a healthy bank can run short: a bank run. Central banks act as lender of last resort, and regulators set liquidity rules. Silicon Valley Bank in the US collapsed in 2023 after a fast, social-media-driven run.

Capital is the shareholders' buffer that absorbs losses before depositors are hurt. International Basel III rules, applied in Sri Lanka by the Central Bank, require banks to hold minimum capital against their risk-weighted assets. Higher capital makes banks safer but can make lending more expensive.

The Central Bank licenses and supervises commercial banks, specialised banks and finance companies. It sets capital and liquidity rules, inspects banks, and can intervene in weak institutions. The largest banks include two state banks, Bank of Ceylon and People's Bank, and private banks such as Commercial Bank, Hatton National Bank and Sampath Bank.

en.title: Deposit insurance in Sri Lanka, India and the US
objectives: Explain what deposit insurance covers and why it exists
Compare coverage limits in Sri Lanka, India and the US
Work out how much of a deposit is protected

learn.body: Deposit insurance promises that small savers will get their money back, up to a limit, if a bank fails. It protects households and makes bank runs less likely, because insured depositors have less reason to rush to withdraw. Most countries have a scheme.

The Sri Lanka Deposit Insurance Scheme, run by the Central Bank, covers deposits at licensed commercial banks, licensed specialised banks and licensed finance companies. Since 2021 it covers up to Rs 1.1 million per depositor per institution. Member institutions pay premiums into the fund; depositors pay nothing directly.

India's Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India, covers up to ₹5 lakh (₹500,000) per depositor per bank, a limit raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020 after the failure of a cooperative bank.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), created in 1933 after waves of bank failures during the Great Depression, covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. Credit unions have a similar scheme through the NCUA.

learn.h: What is covered and what is not
learn.body: Schemes generally cover savings, current and fixed deposits. They do not cover shares, bonds, unit trusts, insurance policies or money lent to unlicensed institutions. Check the exact rules, including how joint accounts and foreign currency deposits are treated, on the scheme's own website.

Because cover is per institution, someone with more than the limit can spread deposits across several licensed institutions to keep each within the insured amount. Moving money between branches of the same bank does not help, because cover is per institution, not per branch.

If depositors know they are protected, they may not care how risky their bank is, and banks may take more risks. That is called moral hazard. Limits, risk-based premiums and strong supervision are ways to reduce it. In 2023 US authorities chose to protect all depositors at Silicon Valley Bank, which renewed this debate.

en.title: Digital payments: LankaQR, UPI, cards
objectives: Describe Sri Lanka's main digital payment systems
Compare cards, QR payments and instant transfers
Explain who pays the costs of different payment methods

learn.body: Cash is still widely used in Sri Lanka, but digital payments have grown fast, especially since COVID-19. They are quicker, leave a record and reduce the risks of carrying cash. They also need a bank account or wallet, a phone or card, and trust in the system.

LankaClear runs the LankaPay network, which links banks for ATM sharing, cards and transfers. Its Common Electronic Fund Transfer Switch (CEFTS) lets people send money instantly between accounts at different banks, any time of day, using account numbers or mobile numbers through banking apps and JustPay.

LankaQR, launched in 2018 by the Central Bank and LankaClear, is a national QR code standard. A shop shows one code that customers can scan with any participating bank or wallet app. Payments go straight from the customer's account to the merchant's, usually at lower cost to the merchant than cards.

Debit and credit cards run on international networks such as Visa and Mastercard, and on LankaPay's national card scheme. Merchants pay a merchant discount rate (MDR), a percentage of each sale, to the card acquirer. Contactless 'tap to pay' and online card payments have spread quickly.

India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India, lets anyone pay instantly from a bank account using a phone number or QR code, usually free for users. It now handles billions of payments every month and is a global example of public digital infrastructure. Since 2024, Indian visitors can pay with UPI at many Sri Lankan merchants.

Mobile network operators and fintech firms offer wallets that hold small balances and pay bills. Around the world, systems such as Kenya's M-Pesa, China's Alipay and WeChat Pay, Brazil's Pix and the US's FedNow and Zelle show different paths to digital payments.

Digital payments are not free: someone pays fees, data and technology costs. Users must protect their PINs and phones, and system outages can stop payments. For people without smartphones, bank accounts or digital skills, keeping cash and simple options available matters. Day 18 covers fraud.

en.title: Fraud and staying safe
objectives: Recognise common financial scams
Explain why pyramid and Ponzi schemes must collapse
Know how to protect accounts and where to report fraud

learn.body: Fraudsters pretend to be your bank, a courier, a government office or a well-known company. They send emails (phishing), call (vishing) or text (smishing) with urgent messages: 'your account will be blocked', 'you have won a prize', 'confirm this payment'. The goal is to get your card details, passwords or one-time passwords (OTPs).

A bank will never ask for your PIN, password or OTP by phone, SMS, email or social media. An OTP is like a key that approves a payment; whoever has it can move your money. If anyone asks for one, end the contact and call your bank on the number printed on your card.

In a SIM swap, a fraudster convinces a mobile operator to move your number to a new SIM, then receives your OTPs. Warning signs include your phone suddenly losing signal. Use strong, unique passwords, app-based or biometric security where available, and set transaction alerts.

A pyramid scheme pays members mainly for recruiting others; a Ponzi scheme pays 'returns' to earlier investors from new investors' money. Both must collapse when recruitment slows, and most people lose. The Central Bank has declared several schemes prohibited, including some that promised high returns through online platforms or digital tokens.

Fake trading apps and crypto platforms show impressive gains on screen but block withdrawals. Romance scammers build online relationships over weeks, then ask for money for an emergency, customs fees or an 'investment'. Many victims are lonely, retired or new to the internet.

Be suspicious of guaranteed high returns, pressure to act fast, requests for secrecy, payment by gift cards or crypto, unlicensed firms, and offers that come to you unasked. Check licences with the Central Bank, the Securities and Exchange Commission or the insurance regulator before investing.

Act fast. Call your bank to block cards and accounts, change passwords, and report to the police (the CID's Computer Crimes Division handles online fraud), the Central Bank's Financial Consumer Relations Department, and Sri Lanka CERT for cyber incidents. Speed can sometimes stop a transfer. Do not be ashamed: fraudsters are professionals.

en.title: Remittances and foreign currency for families
objectives: Compare formal and informal ways to send money home
Calculate the full cost of a remittance including the exchange margin
Describe foreign currency accounts available to Sri Lankans

learn.body: More than a million Sri Lankans work abroad, mainly in the Gulf, and the money they send home pays for food, education, housing and debt across the country. You saw in Economics Foundation that remittances are often Sri Lanka's largest source of foreign currency. For families, choosing how to send and hold that money matters.

Formal channels include bank transfers, licensed money transfer operators and exchange houses, and digital apps linked to banks. Money arrives in a bank account or for cash collection, the transfer is recorded, and the family can use the record to show income when borrowing.

Informal systems, called hawala or undiyal, move value through networks of agents without moving money across borders. They can be fast and offer better rates, but they are illegal for this use in Sri Lanka, give no protection if money is lost, and starve the country of foreign currency. During the 2022 crisis the gap between official and informal rates drew money into these channels.

The cost of sending money is the fee plus the exchange-rate margin: the gap between the rate you get and the market mid-rate. The World Bank tracks costs worldwide; the global average is around 6% of the amount sent, and the UN's Sustainable Development Goal target is below 3%. Comparing the amount the family actually receives is the simplest test.

Sri Lankan banks offer accounts that hold foreign currency. Non-Resident Foreign Currency (NRFC) accounts are for Sri Lankans working abroad; Personal Foreign Currency Accounts (PFCA) are for residents. They let families keep savings in dollars or other currencies and convert to rupees when needed. Rules on use and conversion are set under the Foreign Exchange Act.

Holding some savings in foreign currency can protect a family if the rupee falls, as it did in 2022. But currencies also move the other way: the rupee strengthened in 2023–24, which reduced the rupee value of dollar savings. Spreading conversions over time, rather than converting everything at once, reduces the risk of a bad rate.

Many migrant families spend most remittances on daily needs and consumer goods. Setting a plan, such as part for monthly needs, part for an emergency fund, and part for long-term goals like housing or education, turns years of hard work abroad into lasting security. Some banks offer special savings and housing loan products for migrant workers.

en.title: Islamic banking basics
objectives: Explain the principles behind Islamic finance
Describe common Islamic finance contracts
Compare Islamic and conventional products on cost and risk

learn.body: Islamic finance follows Shariah principles. It prohibits riba (interest), excessive uncertainty (gharar) and investment in forbidden activities such as alcohol and gambling. Instead of lending money for interest, Islamic banks earn returns by trading, leasing or sharing in profits and losses of real economic activity.

In murabaha, the bank buys an asset, such as a vehicle or machine, and sells it to the customer at an agreed higher price, paid in instalments. The profit margin is fixed and disclosed at the start. It is widely used for vehicle, consumer and trade finance.

In ijara, the bank buys an asset and leases it to the customer for rent. In ijara wa iqtina (lease ending in ownership), ownership passes to the customer at the end. It works much like conventional leasing, but the bank owns the asset and bears ownership risks during the lease.

In mudaraba, one party provides capital and the other manages the business; profits are shared in an agreed ratio, and losses fall on the capital provider. Islamic savings accounts often use mudaraba, so returns vary. In musharaka, both parties contribute capital and share profits and losses, used for business and home finance.

Takaful is cooperative insurance: participants contribute to a shared fund that pays claims, with the operator paid a fee. Sukuk are Islamic bonds that give investors ownership in assets or projects and pay returns from them. Governments and companies in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Gulf issue large amounts of sukuk.

Amendments to the Banking Act in 2005 allowed Islamic banking in Sri Lanka. Amana Bank is a licensed commercial bank operating fully on Islamic principles, and several banks and finance companies run Islamic windows. Islamic finance is open to everyone, not only Muslims, and some customers choose it for its asset-backed approach.

An Islamic product's profit rate can cost about the same as a conventional loan's interest rate; compare the total amount repaid, fees and terms. The main differences are legal structure, who owns the asset, how late payments are treated (often penalties go to charity) and, for savings, whether returns are fixed or shared.
