en.title: What a bond is
objectives: Explain the parts of a bond: face value, coupon, maturity and yield
Explain why bond prices fall when yields rise
Describe credit risk and credit ratings

learn.body: A bond is a loan to a government or company that is split into pieces investors can buy and sell. The issuer promises to pay interest, called the coupon, at set times and to repay the face value (also called par or principal) on the maturity date. Bonds let governments and firms borrow from many investors at once.

A Rs 100,000 bond with a 10% coupon, paid half-yearly, maturing in 5 years pays Rs 5,000 every six months and Rs 100,000 at the end. The coupon rate is fixed when the bond is issued. The bond's price in the market can be above par (at a premium) or below par (at a discount).

The yield is the return an investor earns if they buy at today's price and hold to maturity. The current yield is the annual coupon divided by the price: a Rs 10,000 coupon on a bond priced at Rs 95,000 gives about 10.5%. Yield to maturity also counts the gain or loss between the price paid and par.

learn.h: Prices and yields move in opposite directions
learn.body: When market interest rates rise, new bonds pay more, so existing bonds with lower coupons become less attractive and their prices fall. When rates fall, existing bonds become more valuable. A bond's price is the present value of its future payments, so a higher discount rate means a lower price.

The longer the time to maturity, the more a bond's price changes when yields change, because more payments are discounted for longer. A measure called duration captures this. Short-term bonds are less sensitive, which is why cautious investors favour them when rates may rise.

Credit risk is the chance the issuer will not pay. Agencies such as S&P, Moody's and Fitch, and in Sri Lanka Fitch Ratings Lanka and Lanka Rating Agency, rate bonds from AAA (very safe) down to D (default). Riskier issuers must offer higher yields. Bonds rated BBB− or above are called investment grade.

In April 2022 Sri Lanka stopped paying its foreign debt, including its international sovereign bonds, for the first time in its history. Bondholders later accepted a restructuring with losses in late 2024. Defaults show that even government bonds carry risk, especially when they are in foreign currency.

en.title: Treasury bills and bonds
objectives: Explain how Sri Lankan Treasury bills and bonds work
Calculate the return on a Treasury bill bought at a discount
Explain how individuals can invest and what risks remain

learn.body: The government finances its budget deficit and repays old debt by borrowing. In rupees, it mainly issues Treasury bills and Treasury bonds, sold through the Central Bank's Public Debt Department. Banks, pension funds, insurers, companies and individuals buy them.

Treasury bills (T-bills) are short-term: 91, 182 and 364 days. They pay no coupon. Instead, they are sold at a discount and repaid at face value; the difference is the return. They are auctioned every week, and the auction results show the yields the market demands.

Treasury bonds are longer-term, typically from 2 to 20 years or more, and pay a fixed coupon every six months, with the face value repaid at maturity. Their prices move with market yields, as you saw yesterday, so selling before maturity can bring a gain or a loss.

Individuals usually buy through primary dealers or licensed commercial banks, often with a minimum amount, or indirectly through money market and gilt unit trusts. Holdings are recorded electronically in the Central Bank's LankaSecure system. Some institutions offer repurchase agreements (repos) backed by Treasury securities for shorter terms.

Rupee Treasury securities are backed by the government and are generally the safest rupee investment. But in 2023 Sri Lanka's domestic debt optimisation restructured some rupee bonds, mainly those held by superannuation funds such as the EPF, to share the burden of the debt crisis. Inflation and price changes before maturity are also risks.

learn.h: Around the region and the world
learn.body: India's Reserve Bank lets individuals buy government securities directly through its Retail Direct platform. US Treasury bills, notes and bonds are the world's main safe asset, and their yields influence borrowing costs everywhere. When US yields rise, money often flows out of emerging markets such as Sri Lanka.

Plotting yields against maturity gives the yield curve. Usually longer maturities pay more, because investors want extra return for locking money away longer. An inverted curve, where short yields are above long ones, often signals that markets expect rates, and perhaps growth, to fall.

en.title: What a company is
objectives: Compare sole traders, partnerships and limited companies
Explain limited liability and who controls a company
Calculate ownership shares, dividends and market value

learn.body: A sole trader owns and runs the business alone and is personally liable for all its debts. A partnership is owned by two or more people who share profits and, usually, liability. A company is a separate legal person: it can own property, sign contracts, borrow and be sued in its own name.

In a limited liability company, shareholders can lose only what they invested. If the company fails owing more than it owns, creditors cannot claim the shareholders' homes or savings. This protection encourages people to invest in risky ventures and is one of the most important ideas in modern economics.

In Sri Lanka, companies are formed under the Companies Act No. 7 of 2007 and registered with the Registrar of Companies. Private companies, ending in '(Pvt) Ltd', cannot offer shares to the public. Public companies end in 'PLC'; those listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange can have thousands of shareholders and must publish regular financial reports.

A company's ownership is divided into shares. Each share usually gives one vote at general meetings and a right to dividends. Owning 2,000 of 100,000 shares means owning 2% of the company. Shareholders elect the board of directors, approve accounts and decide on big changes.

The board of directors sets strategy and oversees management; the chief executive and managers run daily operations. Good corporate governance means independent directors, honest reporting and protection of minority shareholders. The Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka and the CSE set rules for listed companies.

Companies raise money by issuing shares (equity) or borrowing through loans and bonds (debt). Debt must be repaid with interest whatever happens; equity holders get dividends only if the company does well, but share in all the upside. A first sale of shares to the public is an initial public offering (IPO).

Large Sri Lankan listed groups such as John Keells Holdings, Hayleys and Dialog Axiata run hotels, plantations, retail, telecoms and manufacturing. Globally, the largest companies by market value include Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia in the US, and Reliance Industries and Tata Consultancy Services in India.

en.title: The income statement
objectives: Read the main lines of an income statement
Calculate gross, operating and net profit and their margins
Calculate earnings per share and growth rates

learn.body: The income statement (also called the statement of profit or loss) shows a company's revenue and expenses over a period, usually a quarter or a year, and the profit left at the end. It answers one question: did the business make money in this period, and how?

Revenue is the money earned from selling goods and services. Cost of sales is the direct cost of producing them: materials, factory labour, purchased goods. Revenue minus cost of sales is gross profit. Gross margin, gross profit as a share of revenue, shows how much the company keeps from each rupee of sales before overheads.

Operating expenses include selling and distribution, administration, rent and depreciation, the cost of wearing out equipment spread over its life. Gross profit minus operating expenses is operating profit, also called profit from operations or roughly EBIT (earnings before interest and tax). It shows how well the core business performs.

learn.h: Finance costs, tax and net profit
learn.body: Finance costs are interest on borrowings. Operating profit minus finance costs (plus any finance income) gives profit before tax. After income tax, at a standard corporate rate of 30% in Sri Lanka, comes profit after tax, or net profit. This is what belongs to shareholders.

Earnings per share (EPS) is net profit divided by the number of shares. A company earning Rs 84 million with 40 million shares has EPS of Rs 2.10. Investors compare EPS over time and with the share price; tomorrow's lesson introduces the price-to-earnings ratio.

Margins let you compare companies of different sizes: a supermarket might have a net margin of 2–3%, a software firm 20% or more. Growth rates compare this year with last year. Rising revenue with falling margins can mean a company is buying sales by cutting prices or that its costs are rising faster than its prices.

Profit includes items that are not cash, such as depreciation, and sales made on credit that have not yet been paid. A profitable company can still run out of cash. That is why the cash flow statement, covered tomorrow with the rest of the annual report, matters as much as the income statement.

en.title: Reading an annual report
objectives: Find your way around an annual report
Use the balance sheet and cash flow statement alongside the income statement
Calculate simple ratios and spot warning signs

learn.h: What is in an annual report
learn.body: Listed companies publish an annual report within months of their year end. It typically contains the chairman's and CEO's messages, a management discussion and analysis, sustainability and governance reports, risk management, the auditor's report, and the audited financial statements with notes. The numbers are at the back; start there, then read the story.

The statement of financial position (balance sheet) shows, at the year-end date, what the company owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the shareholders' equity. It always balances: assets = liabilities + equity. Current assets and liabilities are those expected to turn into cash, or be paid, within a year.

The cash flow statement shows cash in and out under three headings: operating activities (from the business itself), investing activities (buying or selling assets) and financing activities (borrowing, repaying, issuing shares, paying dividends). Healthy companies usually generate cash from operations that is close to or above their profit.

learn.h: Read the notes and the auditor
learn.body: The notes explain accounting choices, break down large numbers, and reveal debts, related-party dealings and legal cases. The auditor's report states whether the accounts give a true and fair view. An unqualified (clean) opinion is normal; a qualified opinion, or an emphasis of matter about 'going concern', is a serious warning.

The current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) shows short-term safety; above 1 is usually comfortable. Debt-to-equity shows how much the company relies on borrowing. Return on equity (net profit ÷ equity) shows how well it uses shareholders' money. The price-to-earnings ratio (share price ÷ EPS) and dividend yield (dividend ÷ price) link the accounts to the share price.

Watch for profits that grow while operating cash flow shrinks, rising debt without matching growth, large unexplained 'other' items, frequent changes of auditors or accounting policies, big transactions with related parties, and repeated delays in publishing results. None proves wrongdoing, but each deserves a question.

Read what management says about strategy, risks and outlook, then check it against the numbers and against last year's promises. Sustainability reports cover environmental and social impact, increasingly reported under international standards. Comparing two or three years side by side tells you far more than one year alone.

en.title: Retirement savings: EPF and ETF
objectives: Explain how EPF and ETF work in Sri Lanka
Estimate retirement savings from contributions and returns
Compare retirement systems in India and the US

learn.body: Sri Lankans are living longer, and the population is ageing faster than in most of South Asia. Many people will spend 20 years or more in retirement. Without savings, they depend on family, who may also be stretched. Starting early, as you saw with compounding, makes the biggest difference.

Private sector and many state enterprise employees are members of the EPF. Each month, the employee contributes at least 8% of gross earnings and the employer at least 12%, a total of 20%. The fund is managed by the Central Bank's Monetary Board, invests mainly in government securities, and credits members' accounts with a return declared each year.

Employers also pay 3% of employees' earnings into the Employees' Trust Fund, managed by the ETF Board. There is no employee contribution. ETF balances can be withdrawn on leaving employment after certain periods and at retirement, and the fund offers some welfare benefits.

EPF balances are usually paid out at retirement age: 55 for men and 50 for women, or earlier in specific cases such as permanent disability or leaving Sri Lanka permanently; check the current rules with the EPF Department. In some cases members can use part of their balance to secure a housing loan. Check your balance regularly; employers that fail to pay contributions are breaking the law.

Many government employees receive a public service pension instead of EPF. Self-employed people and informal workers, a large share of Sri Lanka's workforce, have no automatic scheme and must save for themselves, for example through voluntary pension schemes, fixed deposits, Treasury bills or unit trusts.

India's EPF also requires employer and employee contributions (12% each of basic pay), with the National Pension System (NPS) available to all. In the US, Social Security pays a basic state pension funded by payroll taxes, and many workers save in employer 401(k) plans or individual retirement accounts, often invested in shares.

A common guide is to aim for retirement income of around 70% of your final salary. EPF alone may not achieve that, especially if returns barely beat inflation, as you saw on day 10, or if the fund is affected by events such as the 2023 domestic debt optimisation. Most people will need extra savings of their own.

en.title: What markets are
objectives: Explain what a financial market is and why it exists
Name the main types of financial market
Explain how prices in markets carry information

learn.h: A meeting place for buyers and sellers
learn.body: A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers trade. The Pettah wholesale market and an online shop are markets for goods. Financial markets trade claims on money: shares, bonds, currencies, and contracts based on commodities such as oil, gold and tea. Today most financial trading happens on screens, not trading floors.

Financial markets move money from people who have it to people who can use it productively. A company raises money by selling shares; a government borrows by selling bonds; a saver earns a return by buying them. Markets also let people manage risk, for example an importer locking in an exchange rate.

The stock (equity) market trades shares in companies. The bond (debt) market trades loans to governments and companies. The money market deals in very short-term borrowing such as Treasury bills. The foreign exchange market trades currencies. Commodity markets trade raw materials. Derivatives markets trade contracts whose value depends on these.

Market prices combine the views of many buyers and sellers. When a company's share price falls sharply, it signals that investors expect lower profits or more risk. When bond yields rise, it signals that lenders want more for lending. Learning to read these signals is the main skill of this programme.

A liquid market is one where you can buy or sell quickly without moving the price much. Large markets such as US government bonds and major currencies are very liquid. Many shares on smaller exchanges, including the Colombo Stock Exchange, trade only a few times a day, so a large order can move the price a lot.

Investors buy assets for their long-term income and growth. Speculators try to profit from short-term price moves. Hedgers use markets to reduce risks they already face. All three are needed: speculators add liquidity, but heavy speculation can also fuel bubbles and crashes.

Markets are linked to the real economy but are not the same as it. Share prices look ahead, so they often fall before a recession and rise before a recovery. In 2022 the Colombo market fell sharply during the crisis, then rose strongly as inflation fell and the IMF programme took hold.

en.title: Stock exchanges
objectives: Explain what a stock exchange does
Describe how exchanges evolved from trading floors to electronic systems
Compare major exchanges by size

learn.body: A stock exchange is an organised market where shares and other securities are listed and traded under common rules. It provides a trading system, sets listing requirements, publishes prices and company announcements, and monitors trading for abuse. Investors trade through brokers who are members of the exchange.

Early exchanges grew from traders meeting in coffee houses and under trees: London in the 1700s, New York's Buttonwood Agreement in 1792, the Bombay Stock Exchange in 1875. Today trading is almost fully electronic: computers match buy and sell orders in fractions of a second.

To list, a company must meet rules on size, profit history, governance and the share of stock held by the public. Listed companies must publish results, annual reports and price-sensitive news promptly. Listing gives access to more investors and capital, but brings scrutiny and costs.

Share trading in Colombo dates back to the Colombo Share Brokers' Association in 1896. The Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) took its current form in 1985 and introduced automated trading in 1997. It lists around 280 companies. Week 2 looks at it in detail.

The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq in the US are the largest by the value of listed companies. Other major exchanges include those in Shanghai, Shenzhen, Tokyo, Hong Kong, London and India's National Stock Exchange (NSE) and BSE. India's markets have grown rapidly and are now among the five largest in the world.

Many exchanges are themselves listed companies that earn fees from trading, listing and data. The CSE is a company limited by guarantee owned by its members, and plans have been discussed to demutualise it, turning it into a shareholder-owned company.

Not everything trades on an exchange. Over-the-counter (OTC) markets let dealers trade directly with each other by phone or electronic networks. Most bonds and currencies trade OTC. Prices are less visible, which is one reason regulators push more trading onto exchanges.

en.title: Primary and secondary markets
objectives: Distinguish primary and secondary markets
Explain how an IPO and a rights issue work
Calculate proceeds, dilution and the price after a rights issue

learn.body: In the primary market, securities are sold for the first time and the money goes to the issuer: a company selling new shares or a government selling new bonds. In the secondary market, investors trade existing securities with each other; the company receives nothing from these trades. Stock exchanges are mainly secondary markets.

Investors are more willing to buy new shares if they know they can sell them later. A liquid secondary market makes primary issues easier and cheaper. Secondary prices also tell companies what investors think, and set the price for future issues.

An IPO is a company's first sale of shares to the public. The company appoints managers, publishes a prospectus describing its business, risks and finances, and sets a price or price range. Investors apply, shares are allotted, and trading begins on the exchange. If demand is high, the issue is oversubscribed and applicants may get fewer shares than they asked for.

Listed companies raise more money through rights issues, offering new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, usually at a discount. Shareholders can buy, sell their rights, or let them lapse. Private placements sell shares to selected investors. Both increase the number of shares.

Issuing new shares reduces each existing share's slice of the company, called dilution. If you own 1,000 of 100,000 shares (1%) and the company issues 25,000 new shares that you do not buy, you now own 1,000 of 125,000, or 0.8%. Dilution is fine if the new money earns a good return.

Governments and companies also use primary markets for debt. The government auctions Treasury bills and bonds (week 3). Companies issue listed debentures, which then trade on the CSE. In 2021 Sri Lanka's market had several IPOs; across Asia, India's IPO market has been among the world's busiest.

IPO prices are set by the company and its advisers, who want a high price. Some IPOs rise on the first day; many underperform over the following years. Read the prospectus, especially the use of proceeds and risk factors, and be wary of hype.

en.title: Orders and prices
objectives: Read bid and ask prices and an order book
Choose between market and limit orders
Explain how trades set prices and why prices can jump

learn.body: The bid is the highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay; the ask (or offer) is the lowest price a seller will accept. The gap between them is the spread. In busy shares the spread may be a few cents; in thinly traded shares it can be several percent, which is a hidden cost of trading.

The exchange's order book lists all waiting buy and sell orders at each price, with the quantities. A trade happens when a buy order and a sell order meet at the same price. The last traded price is what appears on news tickers, but the order book shows how much you could actually buy or sell, and at what price.

A market order says 'buy (or sell) now at the best available price'. It executes quickly but you do not control the price. In a thin market, a large market order can 'walk the book', filling at progressively worse prices.

A limit order sets the worst price you will accept: buy at no more than Rs 50, or sell at no less than Rs 55. It may not fill if the market does not reach your price, but it protects you from paying too much. Most investors in less liquid markets should use limit orders.

Prices move when buyers or sellers become more eager. News that raises expected profits brings more buyers, who accept higher asks; bad news brings sellers who accept lower bids. Prices can jump overnight when news arrives while the market is closed, opening well above or below the previous close.

To slow panics, exchanges use price bands that limit how far a share can move in a session, and market-wide circuit breakers that pause all trading after a large index fall. The CSE, India's exchanges and US exchanges all use such rules, with different thresholds; check each exchange's current rules.

Volume is the number of shares traded; turnover is their value. A price move on high volume says more than the same move on a few trades. On the CSE, a handful of trades can move a small company's price sharply, so check volume before reading too much into a price change.

en.title: Brokers and CDS accounts
objectives: Explain the roles of stockbrokers and the Central Depository
Describe how to open an account and place a trade in Sri Lanka
Calculate trading costs and their effect on returns

learn.body: Individuals cannot trade directly on the CSE. They trade through licensed stockbroking firms that are members of the exchange. Brokers enter orders, handle money and shares, and many provide research and advice. In Sri Lanka they are licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Shares on the CSE are held electronically in the Central Depository Systems (CDS), set up in 1991. Each investor has a CDS account, opened through a broker, which records the shares they own. Paper share certificates are no longer needed, which makes trading faster and safer.

To start, you choose a broker, complete the account forms with identity documents, and open a CDS account. Many brokers and the CSE's own app now allow online account opening. Foreign investors and Sri Lankans abroad use special accounts linked to foreign currency, under exchange control rules.

You place an order through the broker's app, website or by phone, choosing the share, quantity, buy or sell, and order type. After the trade, you receive a contract note showing the price, quantity, fees and settlement date. Check it carefully against your order.

Each trade carries brokerage commission plus exchange, CDS and regulatory fees and a levy. On the CSE, total costs for small trades have been about 1.1% of the trade value each way (check the current schedule). Buying and later selling costs around 2.2% in total, so frequent trading eats into returns quickly.

Check your CDS statements regularly to confirm that your holdings match your broker's records. Never give a broker blank signed forms or let them trade without your clear instructions. Unauthorised trading is a common complaint; the SEC and CSE handle such complaints.

In India, investors use demat accounts with depositories NSDL and CDSL, through brokers including low-cost online platforms. In the US, many online brokers charge no commission on share trades and earn money in other ways, such as payments for routing orders. Cheap trading has brought in millions of new investors, and also more short-term speculation.

en.title: Who regulates markets
objectives: Name the main market regulators in Sri Lanka, India and the US
Explain what insider trading and market manipulation are
Describe how regulators protect investors

learn.body: Markets work only if investors trust that prices are fair and information is honest. Without rules, insiders could trade on secret information, promoters could pump up prices and dump shares, and companies could hide losses. Regulators set and enforce rules to prevent this.

The Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC), set up in 1987 and now governed by the SEC Act No. 19 of 2021, regulates the securities market: the CSE, brokers, unit trusts and listed companies' disclosures. The Central Bank regulates banks, finance companies and the government securities market. The Insurance Regulatory Commission covers insurers.

The CSE writes and enforces listing rules and trading rules, watches trading for unusual patterns through market surveillance, and can suspend a share. Exchanges are called self-regulatory organisations because they police their own markets under the regulator's oversight.

India's Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), given statutory powers in 1992, regulates its stock markets. The US Securities and Exchange Commission, created in 1934 after the 1929 crash, is the model for many regulators worldwide. Both can fine, ban and prosecute wrongdoers.

Insider trading is buying or selling on important information that is not yet public, such as unannounced results or a takeover. It is illegal because it cheats other investors. Directors and employees must not trade during set periods before results, and must report their dealings.

Manipulation includes spreading false rumours, trading among friends to create fake volume, and 'pump and dump' schemes where promoters hype a small share, then sell to the buyers they attract. Small, thinly traded shares are most at risk. Sudden price jumps with no news deserve caution.

Regulators require disclosure, license intermediaries, handle complaints and run investor education. Sri Lanka's SEC maintains a compensation fund for investors who lose money through broker failure or fraud, within limits. Protection is not a guarantee against losses from ordinary price falls: market risk stays with the investor.

en.title: The Colombo Stock Exchange
objectives: Describe the CSE's size, structure and main participants
Explain the roles of local and foreign investors
Read the CSE's daily market summary

learn.body: The CSE lists around 280 companies across 20 industry groups. A few large companies, mainly banks, diversified groups and consumer firms, make up a large share of the market's value. Many listed companies are small, with few shares in public hands and thin trading.

learn.h: Main Board and Diri Savi Board
learn.body: Companies list on the Main Board, which has stricter size and track-record requirements, or the Diri Savi Board, designed for smaller and growing companies. There is also an Empower Board for small and medium enterprises. Listing rules set minimum public shareholdings, and companies that fall short may be moved to a watch list.

Local individuals make up a large share of trading on many days, alongside local institutions such as unit trusts, insurers and the EPF, and foreign investors. Foreign funds often focus on the largest, most liquid shares. Daily reports show foreign buying and selling, which traders watch closely.

When foreign investors sell more than they buy, called net foreign selling, it can push prices down and add to pressure on the rupee as they convert proceeds to dollars. Net foreign buying does the opposite. Foreign flows into Sri Lanka depend on global risk appetite, US interest rates and Sri Lanka's own economic outlook.

After each session, the CSE publishes the ASPI and S&P SL20 index levels and changes, turnover, volume, the number of trades, the top gainers and losers, and net foreign flows. Learning to read these numbers in a minute or two is a basic market skill.

Besides shares, the CSE lists corporate debentures, closed-end funds, and some government securities. It has been working on new products such as exchange-traded funds and real estate investment trusts. A wider range of products could attract more investors and make the market deeper.

By global standards the CSE is small: its total value is a fraction of Sri Lanka's GDP, while in India and the US stock market value exceeds GDP. Deepening the market, with more listings, more local institutional investors and better liquidity, is a long-standing policy goal.

en.title: Indices: ASPI, S&P SL20, Nifty 50, S&P 500
objectives: Explain what a stock market index measures
Compare the ASPI, S&P SL20, Nifty 50, Sensex and S&P 500
Calculate index changes and the effect of weighting

learn.body: A stock market index tracks the combined value of a group of shares, so you can see how 'the market' or a part of it is doing in one number. Indices are used to report market moves, judge fund managers' performance, and build index funds that simply copy them.

Most modern indices are market-capitalisation weighted: larger companies count more. A 5% rise in a company worth Rs 500 billion moves the index far more than a 5% rise in one worth Rs 5 billion. Many use free-float weighting, counting only shares available to the public. The US Dow Jones Industrial Average is an older, price-weighted index.

The All Share Price Index covers all shares listed on the CSE and is weighted by market capitalisation, with a base value of 100 in 1985. Because it includes everything, it is the broadest measure of the Colombo market, but small, thinly traded shares can make it move in odd ways.

The S&P Sri Lanka 20, launched in 2012 with S&P Dow Jones Indices, tracks 20 of the largest and most liquid CSE companies that meet size, liquidity and financial criteria. It is more useful for large investors and for products such as index funds, because its shares can actually be traded in size.

The Nifty 50 tracks 50 large companies on the National Stock Exchange of India; the Sensex tracks 30 on the BSE. Both are free-float weighted and dominated by banks, IT services, energy and consumer firms. They are watched closely in Sri Lanka because India's economy and investors affect the region.

The S&P 500 tracks about 500 large US companies and is the world's most followed index. Technology giants such as Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia make up a large share of it. Moves in the S&P 500 overnight often set the mood for Asian markets the next morning.

Most headline indices are price indices: they ignore dividends. Total return indices add dividends back in. Over long periods the difference is large, because reinvested dividends compound. When comparing a fund with an index, use the total return version.

en.title: Sectors
objectives: Explain how shares are grouped into sectors
Distinguish cyclical and defensive sectors
Calculate sector weights and their effect on an index

learn.body: Companies in the same sector face similar customers, costs and risks, so their shares often move together. Grouping them helps investors compare like with like, spread risk across different parts of the economy, and see which parts of the market are leading or lagging.

The Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS), created by MSCI and S&P, sorts companies into 11 sectors such as financials, information technology, health care, consumer staples and energy, and then into industry groups. The CSE uses GICS industry groups, so its sectors can be compared with markets worldwide.

Banks make up a large share of the CSE's value, followed by capital goods (which include diversified groups), food, beverage and tobacco, materials, consumer services (hotels and leisure), and telecommunications. Plantation companies, which grow tea, rubber and palm oil, sit within food, beverage and tobacco.

Cyclical sectors, such as construction materials, hotels, vehicles and banks, rise and fall strongly with the economy. Defensive sectors, such as food, utilities, telecoms and health care, are steadier, because people keep buying their products in bad times. Investors shift between them as the economic outlook changes.

Bank shares respond to interest rates and bad loans. Hotels follow tourist arrivals. Plantations follow world tea and rubber prices and the rupee. Manufacturers follow energy costs and demand. Reading the news through this lens tells you which sectors a story is likely to move.

When a few sectors dominate an index, the index reflects their fortunes more than the whole economy. The S&P 500 is heavily weighted to technology; the CSE to banks and diversified groups. Sector concentration matters for anyone using an index fund.

Valuation and profit margins differ naturally between sectors: banks, supermarkets and software firms have very different margins. Compare a company with others in the same sector first, then think about whether the sector as a whole is attractive.

en.title: Market capitalisation
objectives: Calculate market capitalisation and free-float value
Classify companies as large, mid or small cap
Compare stock market size with GDP across countries

learn.body: Market capitalisation, or market cap, is the total value the stock market puts on a company: the number of shares multiplied by the share price. A company with 100 million shares at Rs 150 has a market cap of Rs 15 billion. It changes every time the price changes.

learn.h: Market cap is not the company's cash
learn.body: Market cap is what buyers are paying for the shares today, not money the company holds. If the price doubles, the company does not receive any new money. It does, however, make it easier for the company to raise money or use its shares to buy other firms.

Companies are often grouped by size. Large caps are the biggest and usually the most liquid and stable. Small caps can grow faster but are riskier and harder to trade. The cut-offs depend on the market: a large cap in Colombo might be a small cap in New York.

Free-float market cap counts only shares available to the public, excluding shares held by founders, parent companies or the government that rarely trade. Many large CSE companies are majority-owned by a parent group, so their free-float value is much smaller than their full market cap.

Enterprise value adds debt and subtracts cash: it is what it would cost to buy the whole business, including taking on its debts. Two companies with the same market cap can have very different enterprise values if one has much more debt.

Comparing total market cap with GDP shows how important the stock market is in an economy. In the US the ratio is well above 100%, in India around or above 100%, and in Sri Lanka far lower. Very high ratios can also signal that prices are stretched, which is why some investors watch this measure.

Several US technology companies, including Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia, have each been valued at over $3 trillion, more than the GDP of most countries. Saudi Aramco is the largest outside the US. In India, Reliance Industries and HDFC Bank are among the largest. Sri Lanka's largest listed companies are worth a few billion dollars at most.

en.title: Trading hours and settlement
objectives: Know the trading hours of the CSE, NSE and NYSE in Sri Lankan time
Explain settlement cycles such as T+1 and T+2
Understand corporate action dates such as the ex-dividend date

learn.body: Exchanges trade during set hours. The CSE's regular session runs from 9:30 am to 2:30 pm on market days, after a pre-opening session in which orders are collected to set an opening price. India's NSE trades from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm, which is the same time zone as Sri Lanka. Check each exchange's calendar for holidays.

New York's NYSE and Nasdaq trade 9:30 am to 4:00 pm US Eastern time. That is 8:00 pm to 2:30 am in Sri Lanka during the northern winter, and an hour earlier when the US is on daylight saving time. So US moves usually happen while Sri Lanka sleeps, and show up in Asian markets the next morning.

When you buy shares, the trade is agreed on the trade date (T), but the money and shares change hands later, on the settlement date. The CSE settles share trades on T+2, two market days after the trade. Until settlement, the trade is not complete.

Settlement cycles have been shrinking to reduce risk. India moved fully to T+1 in 2023, and the US moved to T+1 in May 2024. Shorter cycles mean less time for something to go wrong between trade and settlement, but require faster payment systems.

Companies announce dividends, rights issues, bonus shares and share splits. Key dates include the announcement, the record date (who is on the register) and the ex-date, the first day the share trades without the entitlement. Because of settlement, buyers must purchase before the ex-date to receive a dividend.

On the ex-dividend date, the share price usually falls by roughly the dividend amount, because new buyers no longer get it. A share at Rs 100 with a Rs 5 dividend might open near Rs 95. This is not a loss: the shareholder receives the Rs 5 separately.

Markets close on public holidays, which in Sri Lanka include monthly Poya days. Trading can also be halted for technical problems, circuit breakers or emergencies, as in April 2022 when the CSE paused trading for several days during the economic crisis.

en.title: World exchanges compared
objectives: Compare developed, emerging and frontier markets
Explain how global investors classify and choose markets
Calculate returns for a foreign investor including currency moves

learn.body: Index providers such as MSCI and FTSE classify markets as developed (for example the US, Japan, the UK), emerging (for example India, China, Brazil) or frontier (smaller or less open markets). Sri Lanka has been classed as a frontier market. The classification depends on economic size, market size and liquidity, and how easy it is for foreigners to invest.

Trillions of dollars in index funds track these benchmarks. When a country is upgraded, for example from frontier to emerging, funds that follow emerging-market indices must buy its shares, bringing in large inflows. Downgrades work the other way. Market rules, capital controls and currency convertibility all affect a country's status.

The US market is the deepest and most liquid in the world, and its companies earn revenue globally. China's Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges are huge, but foreign access has been more limited and government influence is strong. Hong Kong acts as a bridge between China and global investors.

India has become one of the world's largest stock markets, driven by economic growth, a fast-growing base of domestic investors using mobile apps, and steady monthly investments into mutual funds. Domestic flows now often outweigh foreign flows, which makes the market less dependent on foreign money.

Vietnam's market has grown fast and aims for emerging-market status. Bangladesh and Pakistan have frontier markets that faced currency and political pressures. Comparing them with Sri Lanka shows how macroeconomic stability, openness and liquidity shape market development.

A foreign investor's return depends on both the share price and the currency. If Colombo shares rise 20% in rupees but the rupee falls 10% against the dollar, a dollar-based investor gains only about 8%. That is why currency stability matters so much for attracting foreign investment.

Exchange control rules limit how Sri Lankan residents can invest abroad, and these rules have been tightened and relaxed at different times. Unit trusts and some products give indirect exposure. Check the Central Bank's current foreign exchange regulations before attempting to invest overseas.

en.title: Government bills and bonds
objectives: Describe the government securities market and who takes part
Read a table of market yields
Explain why the government bond market matters to all other markets

learn.h: The biggest market in Sri Lanka
learn.body: By value traded, the government securities market is far larger than the stock market. The government borrows trillions of rupees through Treasury bills and bonds to finance its deficit and roll over maturing debt. Banks, the EPF and other pension funds, insurers, unit trusts and companies hold most of it.

Treasury bills (91, 182 and 364 days) are sold at a discount and pay no coupon. Treasury bonds run from about 2 to 20 years and pay coupons every six months. You met both in Finance Foundation; here the focus is on how they trade and what their prices tell you.

After issue, bills and bonds trade between banks and primary dealers, mostly over the counter, with prices reported to the Central Bank. Each day the Central Bank publishes secondary market yields for each maturity. These yields show where the market thinks interest rates are going.

Government yields are the base rate for the whole economy. Banks price loans and deposits off them, companies issuing debentures pay a spread over them, and share investors compare dividend yields and expected returns with them. When government yields jump, borrowing costs and share valuations usually adjust too.

A yield table lists maturities, from 3 months to 10 years or more, with today's yield and the change from the previous day or week, often in basis points. Rising yields mean falling bond prices. Watch the 364-day bill and the 5-year and 10-year bonds as key points on the curve.

Sri Lanka also borrowed in US dollars by issuing international sovereign bonds (ISBs), traded abroad. Their prices are quoted per 100 dollars of face value. During the 2022 default they fell to around 20–30 cents on the dollar; after the 2024 restructuring, new bonds replaced them. ISB prices are a quick measure of global confidence in Sri Lanka.

Foreign investors can buy rupee government securities, within limits. Their holdings rose and fell sharply around crises. When foreigners sell rupee bonds and take dollars home, it adds pressure on the rupee, which links the bond market to the currency market you will study this week.

en.title: How auctions work
objectives: Explain how Treasury auctions set yields
Distinguish competitive and non-competitive bids
Calculate the cut-off and weighted average yield from bids

learn.body: Governments sell new bills and bonds through auctions so that market demand sets the price. The Central Bank's Public Debt Department announces how much it wants to raise for each maturity, invites bids, and accepts the lowest-cost offers. Auction results are a key weekly signal for interest rates.

In Sri Lanka, bids are submitted by primary dealers, licensed banks and firms appointed by the Central Bank to take part in auctions and keep the secondary market working. Individuals and companies bid through them.

A competitive bid states an amount and the yield (or price) the bidder wants. The Central Bank ranks bids from lowest yield (best for the government) to highest and accepts them until it has raised the amount offered. The highest yield accepted is the cut-off yield.

In a multiple-price auction, as used for Sri Lankan Treasury bills and bonds, each successful bidder pays the yield they bid. In a uniform-price auction, used in some countries, all successful bidders get the cut-off yield. The weighted average yield of accepted bids is published and widely quoted.

If bids total more than the amount offered, the auction is oversubscribed, a sign of strong demand. The Central Bank can accept less than offered, or reject all bids, if yields are higher than it considers reasonable. Undersubscribed or rejected auctions signal stress and can push yields up.

Some amount may be issued non-competitively at the weighted average yield, which helps smaller investors. Sri Lanka also uses a second phase, in which primary dealers can buy more at the weighted average yield after the main auction, if the first phase was not fully accepted.

The US Treasury auctions bills, notes and bonds on a regular calendar and publishes the bid-to-cover ratio, total bids divided by the amount accepted. India's Reserve Bank runs auctions for the government. Weak demand at a big US auction can move markets worldwide.

en.title: Interest rates and markets
objectives: Trace how a policy rate change spreads through markets
Explain why rates affect share, bond and currency prices
Read market expectations of future rate moves

learn.body: When the Central Bank changes its policy rate (the Overnight Policy Rate, OPR), it first moves overnight interbank rates, then Treasury bill yields, then bank deposit and lending rates, and eventually spending, investment and inflation. Markets react within minutes; the economy takes months.

Lower policy rates usually pull down bond yields, which raises bond prices. Longer bonds react more. Investors who expect cuts often buy bonds in advance, so yields may fall before the actual decision.

Lower rates usually help shares in three ways: borrowing costs fall, so company profits rise; consumers spend more; and the safer alternative, T-bills and deposits, pays less, pushing savers towards shares. In Sri Lanka, the sharp fall in rates from 2023 helped drive a strong rise in the ASPI.

Bank profits depend on the gap between loan and deposit rates and on bad loans. Falling rates can squeeze margins at first but reduce bad loans and boost lending. Rising rates can widen margins but increase defaults. That is why bank shares react strongly, and sometimes unexpectedly, to rate news.

Higher interest rates can attract foreign money seeking better returns, supporting the currency; lower rates can do the opposite. For small economies, the effect depends on confidence: if investors fear a crisis, even high rates may not stop a currency falling, as in Sri Lanka in early 2022.

Markets move on surprises. If everyone expects a 50 basis point cut and the Central Bank cuts 50, prices may barely move. A bigger or smaller move than expected, or a change in the bank's guidance about the future, causes the real reaction. Read the monetary policy statement for hints.

The US Federal Reserve sets the world's most important interest rate. When it raises rates, the dollar usually strengthens and money tends to flow out of emerging and frontier markets, raising their borrowing costs. Its 2022–23 rate rises contributed to pressure on many developing countries, including Sri Lanka.

en.title: Exchange rates
objectives: Read currency quotes, buying and selling rates and cross rates
Describe how the foreign exchange market is organised
Distinguish spot and forward rates

learn.body: The foreign exchange (FX) market is the largest financial market in the world, with trading of several trillion US dollars every day. It runs 24 hours a day on weekdays, moving from Asia to Europe to the Americas. Banks, companies, investors, central banks and tourists all take part.

A quote such as USD/LKR 300 means one US dollar costs 300 rupees. The first currency is the base, the second the quote currency. EUR/USD 1.10 means one euro costs 1.10 dollars. Most currencies are quoted against the US dollar, which is on one side of nearly 90% of all trades.

Banks show two rates: the buying rate, at which they buy foreign currency from you, and the selling rate, at which they sell it to you. The gap is the bank's margin. Banks in Sri Lanka publish both daily, along with different rates for cash, telegraphic transfers and cards.

Large trades happen between banks in the interbank market, at tighter spreads than customers get. The Central Bank publishes an indicative rate each day based on interbank trading. Newspaper and app quotes usually show this middle rate, not what you would actually get at a counter.

The rate between two currencies that are not the dollar can be worked out through the dollar. If USD/LKR is 300 and USD/INR is 85, then one Indian rupee costs 300 ÷ 85 ≈ 3.53 Sri Lankan rupees. This is how banks price less traded pairs.

The spot rate is for immediate exchange, normally settled within two days. A forward contract fixes a rate today for exchange on a future date, letting importers and exporters remove uncertainty. Forward rates differ from spot mainly because of the interest rate difference between the two currencies.

If rupee interest rates are higher than dollar rates, the forward USD/LKR rate is above the spot rate: the rupee trades at a forward discount. Otherwise, someone could borrow cheap dollars, convert, earn high rupee interest and lock in the return risk-free. The forward premium roughly equals the interest rate difference.

en.title: What moves the rupee
objectives: Identify the flows that create demand for and supply of dollars
Explain how inflation, interest rates and confidence affect the rupee
Analyse a rupee move using balance of payments data

learn.body: The rupee's value against the dollar depends on how many dollars come into Sri Lanka compared with how many are needed. Dollars come in from exports, tourism, remittances, foreign investment and borrowing. They go out for imports, debt repayments, profit payments and money taken abroad.

Imports, especially fuel, are the biggest use of dollars. When oil prices rise or import demand grows, as with the reopening of vehicle imports, more dollars are needed and the rupee tends to weaken. Strong export months, tourist seasons and festive remittances bring in dollars and support it.

Repaying foreign loans and bonds uses dollars. After the 2022 default, debt payments were suspended; as restructured debts begin to be serviced again, regular dollar outflows return. Large repayment dates are known in advance and are watched by markets.

Over the long run, a currency tends to weaken in line with the gap between its inflation and that of its trading partners. If Sri Lankan prices rise 6% a year and US prices 2%, the rupee will tend to lose about 4% a year against the dollar. This idea is called purchasing power parity.

Higher rupee interest rates can attract foreign money into government securities and shares, supporting the rupee. When global rates rise or confidence falls, that money can leave quickly. These 'hot money' flows can move the rupee sharply in a few weeks.

If people expect the rupee to fall, exporters delay converting dollars and importers rush to buy them, which makes the fall happen. Confidence depends on reserves, the IMF programme, politics and policy credibility. In 2022 a collapse in confidence turned a weak rupee into a crisis.

The Central Bank's monthly external sector report shows exports, imports, tourism earnings, remittances, foreign flows to shares and bonds, and reserves. Comparing these with the exchange rate lets you explain most moves. Seasonal patterns, such as higher import demand before festivals, also matter.

en.title: Central bank intervention
objectives: Explain how and why central banks intervene in currency markets
Describe the tools Sri Lanka has used, from reserves to controls
Weigh the costs and benefits of managing the exchange rate

learn.body: A central bank intervenes when it buys or sells foreign currency to influence the exchange rate. Selling dollars from reserves supports the rupee; buying dollars, paying with rupees, holds the rupee down and adds to reserves. Most central banks in emerging economies intervene at least sometimes.

Common reasons are to smooth sharp, disorderly moves, to stop panic, to build reserves when inflows are strong, or to hold a particular rate. Smoothing is widely accepted; holding a rate the economy cannot support usually ends badly, as you saw in Economics Foundation.

After the 2022 crisis, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka bought large amounts of dollars from the market when inflows were strong, rebuilding reserves from very low levels. This kept the rupee from strengthening as much as it otherwise would have, but made the country safer against future shocks.

Besides buying and selling, central banks use interest rates, rules requiring exporters to convert part of their earnings into rupees, limits on how much can be taken out of the country, and import restrictions. Sri Lanka used many of these in 2020–2022, including bans on vehicle imports, which were eased from 2025.

Controls can save dollars in a crisis but bring costs: shortages, black markets, less foreign investment, and businesses unable to get inputs. Relaxing them can bring sudden outflows. Most economists favour a flexible rate with smoothing, adequate reserves and credible policy over long-term controls.

When a central bank buys dollars, it pays with new rupees, which adds money to the banking system and could push down interest rates or raise inflation. It can offset this by selling government securities to absorb the rupees, called sterilisation. This links currency intervention with the money markets you studied this week.

India's Reserve Bank holds large reserves and intervenes often to smooth the rupee. Hong Kong defends a fixed peg to the US dollar. Japan has occasionally sold dollars to support a weak yen. The Swiss National Bank has bought huge amounts of foreign currency to stop the franc becoming too strong.

en.title: Oil
objectives: Explain how oil is priced and traded globally
Identify what moves oil prices
Trace how oil prices affect Sri Lanka's economy and markets

learn.body: Oil fuels transport, power plants and industry and is the raw material for plastics and chemicals. Its price affects inflation, trade balances and growth in almost every country. The world uses around 100 million barrels a day; one barrel is about 159 litres.

Oil is priced against benchmark grades. Brent, from the North Sea, is the main global benchmark, used for most oil sold to Asia and Europe. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the US benchmark. Prices are quoted in US dollars per barrel, and futures contracts on exchanges in London and New York set prices for months ahead.

OPEC+, a group of oil exporters led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, agrees production targets to influence prices. The United States has become the world's largest producer thanks to shale oil. Wars, sanctions and attacks on shipping routes, such as in the Red Sea, can disrupt supply suddenly.

Oil reached about $147 a barrel in 2008, then crashed during the financial crisis. In April 2020, as COVID-19 lockdowns emptied roads, a WTI futures contract briefly traded below zero because storage was full. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Brent rose above $120. Swings of 30% or more in a year are common.

Sri Lanka has no oil production and imports all its crude oil and refined products, making fuel its largest import bill. Ceylon Petroleum Corporation runs the Sapugaskanda refinery and sells fuel alongside Lanka IOC and other licensed retailers. Retail fuel prices are revised monthly using a pricing formula linked to world prices and the exchange rate.

learn.h: How oil moves Sri Lankan markets
learn.body: Higher oil prices raise the import bill, put pressure on the rupee, push up inflation through transport and electricity costs, and can lead to higher interest rates. Shares of transport, power-intensive manufacturers and airlines usually suffer; when oil falls, the reverse happens. The 2022 fuel queues showed how a dollar shortage turns into an oil shortage.

Growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles is slowly reducing oil's share of energy use. For Sri Lanka, more renewable electricity and electric transport could cut the oil import bill and make the economy less exposed to oil shocks, though the transition needs large investment.

en.title: Gold
objectives: Explain how gold is priced in world and local markets
Convert world gold prices into Sri Lankan rupees per pawn
Weigh gold's role as a safe haven against its drawbacks

learn.body: World gold prices are quoted in US dollars per troy ounce, which is about 31.1 grams. The main trading centres are London and New York, with large markets in Shanghai, Mumbai and Dubai. Prices move every second during trading hours.

Gold has been used as money and a store of value for thousands of years. It cannot be printed, does not rust, and is accepted worldwide. Investors buy it as a safe haven in crises and as protection against inflation and currency falls. Central banks hold it as part of their reserves.

Gold tends to rise when real interest rates fall (because holding gold gives up less interest), when the US dollar weakens, when inflation fears grow, and during wars and crises. Heavy buying by central banks, especially China, India, Turkey and Poland, pushed prices to record highs in recent years, above $4,000 an ounce in 2025.

In Sri Lanka gold is a traditional form of saving, mostly as jewellery, and is quoted per pawn (8 grams) in 22 carat and 24 carat. 24 carat is nearly pure; 22 carat is about 91.7% gold. Local prices follow the world price, the exchange rate, and import duties and margins.

Gold is widely used as collateral for pawning loans, from banks, finance companies and pawn brokers. When gold prices rise, people can borrow more against the same jewellery. When prices fall, lenders may ask for more gold or sell pledged items if loans are not repaid.

Gold pays no interest or dividends, so its return comes only from price rises. Jewellery carries making charges that are lost when sold, and buying and selling margins can be large. Gold prices can also fall sharply: after peaking in 2011, gold lost over a third of its value by 2015.

Investors abroad can buy gold through exchange-traded funds, coins and bars, or sovereign gold bonds (as in India). These avoid making charges and storage problems. In Sri Lanka, options beyond jewellery and bars are limited; check what is available and its costs.

en.title: Tea, rubber and coconut
objectives: Explain how the Colombo Tea Auction sets tea prices
Describe the markets for rubber and coconut products
Analyse how commodity prices and the rupee affect plantation companies

learn.body: Most Sri Lankan tea is sold through the Colombo Tea Auction, one of the largest and oldest in the world, held since 1883. Every week, brokers catalogue and sample teas from estates and factories, and exporters bid for each lot. Prices are in rupees per kilogram and published in weekly auction reports.

Ceylon tea is grouped by where it is grown: high grown (over about 1,200 metres), mid grown and low grown. Each has its own flavour, buyers and price trend. Low-grown teas, popular in the Middle East and Russia, have often fetched the highest average prices at auction in recent years.

Demand from key buyers such as Iraq, Turkey, Russia, the UAE and Iran matters most, along with their ability to pay in dollars. Supply depends on weather, fertiliser and labour. Competition comes from Kenya, India and China. A weaker rupee raises rupee auction prices even if dollar prices are unchanged.

Sri Lanka produces about 250 million kilograms of tea a year and earns over a billion dollars from tea exports. Production fell after the 2021 ban on chemical fertiliser and has been recovering. Plantation companies listed on the CSE, managed under long-term leases from the state, depend heavily on tea and rubber prices and wage costs.

Natural rubber is grown mainly in the wet zone. World prices are set on exchanges in Singapore, Tokyo and Shanghai and follow car production and oil prices, since synthetic rubber is made from oil. Sri Lanka's bigger earner is rubber products, such as tyres and gloves, made by manufacturers using local and imported rubber.

Coconut is both a staple food and an export crop. Exports include desiccated coconut, coconut oil, milk, water and coir. Local nut prices swing with rainfall: a drought can cut supply and send prices up a year later, as in 2024–25. High nut prices help growers but hurt households and exporters of coconut products.

Sri Lanka has no local futures exchange for these crops, so producers and exporters face price swings with limited ways to hedge. Long-term contracts, diversifying markets and products, and adding value through branding and packaging, as with branded Ceylon tea, are ways to reduce dependence on auction prices.

en.title: Scams and pyramid schemes
objectives: Recognise investment scams that target market newcomers
Explain why pyramid schemes and guaranteed returns are mathematically impossible to sustain
Check whether an investment offer is licensed and legitimate

learn.body: Rising markets, social media and easy mobile payments attract many first-time investors, and scammers follow them. They use the language of markets, such as trading, forex, crypto, 'AI bots' and 'guaranteed profit', to make schemes sound real. Finance Foundation covered general fraud; today focuses on fake investments.

A pyramid scheme rewards members mainly for recruiting others, not for selling real products. Because each level needs many more members than the last, recruitment runs out quickly and most people lose. In Sri Lanka, the Banking Act prohibits pyramid schemes, and the Central Bank has publicly named several as prohibited, including some disguised as digital token or online trading platforms.

A Ponzi scheme pays 'returns' to earlier investors from new investors' money and invents profits on paper. The name comes from Charles Ponzi in 1920s Boston; Bernard Madoff ran the largest known one, about $65 billion on paper, until 2008. Steady high returns with no losing months are a warning sign.

Unlicensed 'forex', 'crypto' or 'binary options' platforms show rising balances on screen, encourage you to deposit more, then block withdrawals or demand 'taxes' and 'fees' to release funds. Many are run from abroad and impossible to pursue. Neither the SEC nor the Central Bank licenses such retail forex platforms in Sri Lanka.

learn.h: Pump and dump and fake tips
learn.body: Groups on WhatsApp, Telegram and social media push small listed shares with promises of quick gains. Organisers buy first and sell to the followers they attract. Paid 'signal' services and fake screenshots of profits are common tools.

Before investing, check: Is the firm licensed by the SEC, the Central Bank or the insurance regulator? Can you find it on the regulator's website, not just its own? Are returns guaranteed or unusually high? Is there pressure to recruit or act fast? Can you see audited accounts? If any answer is wrong, walk away.

Stop paying, even if told one more payment will unlock your money. Keep records of all messages and payments. Report to the police (including the CID's Financial Crimes Investigation Division or Computer Crimes Division), the Central Bank and the SEC. Warn friends and family, since scams spread through trusted networks.

items.title: Investor alerts and bulletins
items.note: Read one alert about crypto or AI investment fraud.

practise.q: A scheme needs each member to recruit 4 people. Starting from 1 founder, how many members are at level 12?
practise.answer: Over 16.7 million, most of Sri Lanka's adult population.

practise.q: A platform promises 2% a week. What does that compound to over a year?
practise.answer: About 180% a year, no real investment does this reliably.

practise.q: A Ponzi scheme has Rs 500 million of 'investments' and pays 3% a month. How much must it pay out each month?
practise.answer: Rs 15 million a month, all from new money.

practise.q: If new deposits are only Rs 10 million a month, how long until the scheme runs short?
steps: Shortfall: 15 − 10 = 5 million a month, assuming no cash reserve.
practise.answer: Immediately: it falls Rs 5 million behind each month and must collapse.

practise.q: A victim deposits Rs 200,000. The app shows Rs 500,000 and asks for a 20% 'tax' to withdraw. How much more would they lose by paying?
practise.answer: Rs 100,000 more, on top of the Rs 200,000 already gone.

practise.q: A real diversified share fund returned 12%, −8%, 20%, 5% and −3% over five years. What is its simple average return, and does a steady 'guaranteed' 30% a year look realistic?
practise.answer: 5.2% average, with ups and downs. A steady 30% with no bad years is a red flag.

apply.title: Case: the trading club
apply.brief: Rohan's colleague invites him to a 'trading club' that uses an AI bot to trade forex and crypto. Members deposit at least Rs 100,000, see daily profits in an app, and earn bonuses for bringing in new members. The colleague shows screenshots of withdrawals.
questions: List every warning sign in this offer.
Why might the colleague genuinely believe it is real?
What checks could Rohan make in ten minutes, and what should he say to his colleague?

Who ran the largest known Ponzi scheme?
In Sri Lanka, pyramid schemes are prohibited under…
quiz.x: The Central Bank names prohibited schemes.

quiz.p: If each member recruits 3, how many members are at level 5?
A scheme paying 4% a month on Rs 250m must pay out how many Rs million a month?
Which is a warning sign?
o: Guaranteed high returns with no losing months
A licence you can verify on the regulator's site
quiz.x: Real investments go up and down.

quiz.p: Fake trading platforms often…
o: Block withdrawals or demand fees to release funds
quiz.x: Do not pay more to 'unlock' money.

quiz.p: Paying a 'withdrawal tax' to a suspicious platform will usually release your money.
quiz.x: It usually just adds to the loss.

quiz.p: Where should you verify an investment firm's licence?
o: On the firm's own website only
quiz.x: SEC, Central Bank or insurance regulator.

quiz.p: Simple average of returns 10, −5 and 13 (%)?
Pump and dump schemes usually target…
If you have been caught in a scam, you should first…
Scams often spread through friends and family.
1% a day compounded for 30 days multiplies money by about how much (2 decimals)?

en.title: Investor rights
objectives: List the main rights of shareholders and bondholders
Explain how minority shareholders are protected, including in takeovers
Know how to use your rights and where to complain

learn.body: Owning shares gives you rights: to vote at general meetings, including on electing directors; to receive dividends declared; to receive annual reports and other information; to ask questions at the annual general meeting (AGM); and, usually, to buy new shares before outsiders in a rights issue, protecting you from dilution.

Listed companies must hold an AGM each year. Shareholders can attend in person or online, vote directly or by proxy, approve the accounts and dividends, elect directors and appoint auditors. Most small shareholders never attend, but the AGM is the one place they can question the board directly.

Many listed companies have a controlling shareholder. Rules protect minority shareholders from being treated unfairly: related-party transactions above set limits need disclosure and sometimes approval by independent shareholders; major transactions need shareholder approval; and the Companies Act lets shareholders go to court if the company's affairs are run in an oppressive way.

When someone buys enough shares to gain control of a listed company, takeover rules usually require them to offer to buy the remaining shares at a fair price, so minority shareholders can exit. In Sri Lanka the Takeovers and Mergers Code sets this mandatory offer threshold, currently at 30% of voting rights; check the latest code. Independent advice is provided to shareholders.

learn.h: Rights of bondholders and unit holders
learn.body: Bondholders and debenture holders have a legal right to interest and repayment on the agreed terms, often protected by a trustee who can act for them if the issuer defaults. Unit trust holders have rights set out in the trust deed, with a trustee and the SEC overseeing the fund manager.

Start with the company, broker or fund manager in writing. If unresolved, complain to the CSE (for listed companies and brokers) or the SEC, which has an investor complaints process. In India, SEBI runs an online complaints system called SCORES; in the US, the SEC accepts tips and complaints online.

Rights only work if investors use them: read the annual report, vote, attend or watch AGMs, and raise concerns. Institutional investors such as the EPF and unit trusts have a particular duty to engage with companies on behalf of the savers whose money they manage.

practise.q: You own 5,000 of a company's 2 million shares. What percentage of the votes do you hold?
An investor holds 28% and buys another 4%. Does the mandatory offer threshold of 30% apply?
practise.answer: Yes: they would normally have to offer for the remaining shares.

practise.q: A 1-for-5 rights issue: you hold 5,000 shares. How many new shares can you buy?
practise.answer: 1,000 shares, protecting your percentage if you take them up.

practise.q: A company declares a Rs 3.50 dividend. You hold 5,000 shares. What is your gross dividend?
A takeover offer is Rs 75 a share. The share traded at Rs 60 before the announcement. What is the premium?
At an AGM, a resolution gets 62% of votes cast in favour. A special resolution needs 75%. Does it pass as a special resolution?
practise.answer: No: it would pass only as an ordinary resolution (over 50%).

apply.title: Case: the related-party deal
apply.brief: A listed company plans to buy land from a company owned by its chairman's family for Rs 2 billion. Independent valuations suggest the land is worth about Rs 1.4 billion. The chairman's family controls 55% of the company's shares.
questions: Why are minority shareholders worried?
Which rights and rules could protect them?
What could a minority shareholder do before and at the general meeting?

The AGM is where shareholders can…
o: Question the board and vote on resolutions

quiz.p: Owning 10,000 of 4 million shares is what % of votes?
Sri Lanka's mandatory takeover offer threshold is what % of voting rights?

o: Sell their shares when control changes

quiz.p: An offer of Rs 90 for a share trading at Rs 72 is what premium, in %?
Related-party transactions are concerning because…
o: Controlling owners may benefit at others' expense

quiz.p: A debenture trustee…

quiz.x: After writing to the firm first.

Unit trust holders' rights are set out in the trust deed.

en.title: Reading financial news
objectives: Read market reports critically, separating facts from explanations
Spot common traps with numbers, percentages and charts
Build a reliable daily routine for following markets

learn.body: In Sri Lanka, business news comes from newspapers such as the Daily FT, the Sunday Times business section and The Island, from online outlets such as EconomyNext, and from broker research. Regionally and globally, Reuters, Bloomberg, the Financial Times and India's Economic Times are widely used. Official sources, such as the Central Bank, CSE and Department of Census and Statistics, are the base for most stories.

A market report mixes facts ('the ASPI fell 1.2%') with explanations ('on profit-taking after recent gains'). Facts can be checked; explanations are often guesses written after the event. When a report gives a cause, ask whether it is supported by evidence, such as volume, foreign flows or a specific announcement.

A '200-point fall' sounds big, but its meaning depends on the level: 200 points is 1.3% of an index at 15,000 and 0.4% of one at 50,000. Always convert to percentages. Similarly, 'rates rose 50 basis points' means half a percentage point, not 50%.

Year-on-year changes depend on the starting point. After a collapse, a large percentage rise may only return to the old level. Inflation can fall sharply simply because prices jumped a year earlier. Averages can hide extremes: an average return of 10% may include a year of −20%.

Check a chart's axes before drawing conclusions. A y-axis that starts far above zero makes small moves look dramatic. Different time ranges tell different stories: a share that fell this month may have doubled over five years. Look for the source and dates of the data.

Separate news reports from opinion columns, interviews with people who have something to sell, and sponsored content paid for by companies. Social media posts and 'tips' are not news. Ask: who is telling me this, how do they know, and what do they gain if I believe it?

A simple routine: check overnight moves in US and Indian markets and oil; read the CSE market summary and Central Bank rates in the afternoon; skim one local and one international business news source; and note anything that affects your watchlist. Fifteen minutes a day, consistently, builds real understanding over months.

practise.q: A headline says 'ASPI plunges 180 points' with the index at 16,200. What is the percentage fall?
The S&P 500 'drops 60 points' from 6,000. What is the percentage fall?
A share fell 50% last year and rose 60% this year. The headline says 'up 60%!'. Where is it compared with two years ago?
practise.answer: Still 20% below where it was two years ago.

practise.q: Inflation fell from 50% to 10% year on year. Are prices lower than a year ago?
steps: 10% inflation means prices are still 10% higher than a year ago.
practise.answer: No: prices are still rising, just more slowly.

practise.q: A chart's y-axis runs from 15,000 to 15,400 and shows a 'collapse' from 15,380 to 15,050. What is the actual fall?
practise.answer: About 2.1%: the axis makes it look much bigger.

practise.q: A report says yields 'jumped 75 basis points to 9.25%'. What were they before?

apply.title: Case: two stories, one day
apply.brief: On the same day, one news site says 'Colombo stocks fall on political uncertainty' while another says 'Profit-taking pulls ASPI lower after record run'. The CSE data show the ASPI fell 0.8% on below-average turnover, with small net foreign buying.
questions: Which facts do both stories agree on?
Which explanation is better supported by the data, and why?
What extra information would help you decide?

quiz.p: Which is a fact rather than an explanation?
A 150-point fall from 15,000 is what % fall?
A 500-point fall from 50,000 is what % fall?
How many percentage points is 25 basis points?
A base effect means…
o: Percentage changes depend heavily on the starting point
quiz.x: After a collapse, big rises may only recover losses.

quiz.p: Falling inflation means prices are falling.
A y-axis that starts far above zero…
Sponsored content is…

Which is an official source for Sri Lankan market data?
o: The CSE and the Central Bank

Yields rising 50 bp to 10% were what before, in %?
A good question to ask about any market claim is…
o: Who is telling me, how do they know, and what do they gain?

A sensible daily routine includes…
o: Overnight global moves, the CSE summary and one or two news sources

project.title: Capstone: explain one week of market news
project.brief: Choose one recent week. Using official data and news reports, explain what happened across Sri Lanka's markets and why, as if briefing a friend who knows nothing about markets. Present it as a 1,500-word report or a 10-slide presentation.
include: Daily data for the ASPI, S&P SL20, turnover and net foreign flows, with the week's change
T-bill auction results and secondary yields, and the week's change in basis points
USD/LKR at the start and end of the week, with reasons for the move
Brent oil, gold and the latest tea auction prices, and how they affected Sri Lankan markets
At least three news stories, each separated into facts and explanations, with your judgement on the explanation
How your watchlist companies moved, and a one-paragraph outlook for the coming week
rubric: Accurate, dated, sourced data
Correct use of concepts from all four weeks
Clear links between news and market moves
Critical reading of sources
Plain, well-organised explanation a non-specialist can follow
